title: How Nammu21 automates syndicated loans on Google Cloud Universal Ledger
raw_text: The syndicated loan and private credit markets, both critical components of corporate finance, have long been constrained by manual processes, leading to multi-week settlements, valuation opacity, and trade friction. To solve these long-standing challenges, fintech innovator Nammu21 partnered with Google Cloud on a new proof-of-concept. Using its AI-powered platform to structure legal agreements and instantiate them as smart contracts on the Google Cloud Universal Ledger (GCUL) , Nammu21 automates the entire loan lifecycle, paving the way for improved settlement times and greater market efficiency. Digitizing the loan market While loan markets provide billions in capital to businesses worldwide, their underlying infrastructure has not kept pace with the speed of digital finance. This landscape requires continuous coordination across facility agents, borrowers, and diverse lender syndicates, while also managing highly customized credit agreements with dynamic tranches and complex covenants. In particular, relying on fragmented, manual interpretation of legal text often results in significant operational drag and data silos. According to the Loan Market Association , secondary market settlement times for par/near par loans in Q4 2024 still averaged 42 days, with a median of 27 days. These notoriously slow timelines tie up capital, increase counterparty risk, and create a heavy reconciliation burden for participants. Nammu21 transforms bespoke credit documents into programmable assets at scale by rendering each facility's governing terms as a Digital Credit Instrument (DCI). The DCI maps every term — including conditions, consents, eligibility criteria, and operational mechanics that determine what is permitted under a facility — directly back to its originating legal provision. These elements are then expressed as executable behaviours against a loan's live state. To instantiate these instruments, the proof-of-concept utilizes the secure, high-performance execution environment of GCUL, an institutional-grade, permissioned distributed ledger that helps automate complex financial workflows to deliver near-instant transaction finality and predictable costs without the volatility or security concerns of public blockchains. A purpose-built stack for digital credit Combined with Nammu21’s data intelligence, GCUL provides the foundational infrastructure for converting legal document logic into live, programmable contracts. Designed to handle the privacy, scale, and multi-party coordination required by institutional finance, GCUL provides a permissioned, high-performance distributed ledger that delivers deterministic, instant transaction finality for high-value financial settlements. Programmable contracts on GCUL are written in gculpy , GCUL's domain-optimized programming language. As a strict, statically-typed subset of Python, gculpy is designed to be safe, readable, and auditable, making it ideal for processing complex financial logic. For regulated financial institutions, gculpy offers distinct operational advantages over other ledger programming models. The language simplifies development by removing the need for complex memory management or workarounds to meet highly restrictive call stack limits, allowing engineers to focus on the financial logic itself. GCUL also provides robust, built-in permissioning, requiring explicit user authorization before a contract can store data on their behalf. This solves the "unsolicited asset" problem — common on public networks — where unwanted tokens can be sent to an organization's wallet, creating compliance and accounting issues. With GCUL, institutions can maintain full control over which assets they interact with to support their high-value, highly regulated use cases. Nammu21 serves a dual role in this architecture. First, the platform renders the DCI programmatically from the original legal agreement without manual document reading to establish the terms. Next, it derives gculpy contracts that define the structure of the obligation and govern the loan on GCUL, using the DCI to supply the terms that determine what the loan documents permit, require and block. Technical architecture: The loan lifecycle on GCUL Nammu21’s loan implementation on GCUL demonstrates the value of creating a single, immutable source of truth. The proof-of-concept modeled a $1.945 billion Term Loan B — one segment of a broader multi-facility transaction — where the agent bank, borrower, transferor, and transferee all worked off a permissioned view of the same on-ledger rendering. The lifecycle begins when an agent bank selects a specific credit agreement transformed by Nammu21. The platform instantly provides the structured terms from the document, which are used to instantiate a unique gculpy contract on GCUL, establishing a verifiable, on-ledger digital twin of that specific loan facility. Next, the agent bank initiates the onboarding of the borrower and lenders. This multilateral action requires that each participant review the request and then provide explicit consent by approving the onboarding invitation from their own interface. Once all parties are onboarded, the agent bank records an immutable hash of the loan's key terms on-ledger, attesting that the on-ledger data matches the canonical off-ledger records. Subsequent lifecycle events, such as secondary market transfers or repayments, are also managed as multi-step, automated workflows governed by a consent-driven model. For example, a transfer of a loan position requires new lender, borrower, and agent bank consent before it can be executed atomically on the ledger. All payment flows, from interest payments to loan close-outs, settle directly on GCUL using tokenized commercial bank money, eliminating the need for external payment rails. Transacting with familiar, regulated money on a programmable ledger provides an architecture purpose-built for institutional finance, grounded in three core pillars: 1. Compliance via gated execution: Nammu21’s gculpy contracts instantiated with governing terms, validate every action against the terms transformed from the agreement before execution, mitigating potential covenant breaches or invalid transfers upfront while eliminating the risk of silent failures. 2. Role-based privacy: GCUL enforces strict, role-based access, ensuring that trading strategies, positions, and sensitive loan data remain confidential and are visible only to the necessary counterparties in a transaction. 3. Settlement finality: Every on-ledger action completes near-instantly and anchors on canonical data derived from the original credit agreement, replacing provisional, reconciliation-heavy models with real-time, trusted verification. The business impact of moving on-ledger This proof-of-concept illustrates a structural shift in how credit markets can operate. When each facility's governing terms are rendered as a DCI and executed on GCUL, the operational mechanics of lending markets change fundamentally, rather than incrementally. Values can be reconciled bilaterally, but governance logic cannot – and the market’s current friction stems directly from each party's independent interpretation of the rules. Resolving this issue on-ledger is what enables settlement times to compress, back-office overhead to shrink, and counterparty risk to be mitigated by design rather than by manual checking. This same architecture can be applied wherever credit terms are bespoke and manually interpreted. By freeing up capital that would otherwise be trapped in lengthy settlement cycles, new liquidity is unlocked and a more dynamic and efficient secondary loan market can emerge. title: Leading in the agentic era: How to put people first as you adopt AI agents
raw_text: Over the past few years, our Google Cloud Consulting team has partnered with many companies to introduce AI into their daily operations. In that time, we’ve seen the focus shift from generative AI that answers questions to agentic systems that fully carry out the work. These agents can create multi-step plans and manage a project from start to finish. While budget, compute, and tooling can help launch an agent program, enterprise adoption takes intentional culture work. People need to feel empowered enough to experiment with agents, and leaders need to show teams what agents mean for their roles. Based on our work across these organizations, we’ve put together five practical lessons for guiding enterprises through an agentic shift. 1. Make workflows agent-executed, human-directed Most enterprise workflows run like a relay race: one person completes a task, checks it, and hands it off to the next person, who then does the same. Layering an AI agent onto that model gives you a faster runner for one leg, but the handoffs may stall or slow down other work. Redesigning your workflows can remove blockers like these in a few ways: Strategic direction: Move from human-in-the-loop validation (where a person checks each step) to a human-in-the- lead model. Agents take on the work, and people set the direction and own the outcomes. Parallel dependencies: One agent can handle every dependency at once instead of passing work through a multi-person queue. For example, an agent can check product availability, credit limits, and contract paperwork at the same time without waiting on each step to finish. Manage by exception: Once the process is set up this way, the agent absorbs routine deterministic transactions, routing only ambiguous or high-judgment scenarios to human review. Cross-team stalls disappear, and your team stays in control. 2. Turn hesitation into ownership In our experience, the biggest barrier to adoption is trust. Many employees worry about their value if an agent handles most of their day-to-day tasks. Others are concerned with who takes the blame if an agent makes a mistake. We encourage teams to treat agents the way they'd treat a junior team member: Active delegation: Frame agents as digital coworkers. That means assigning tasks to them, defining their scope, and checking their work for accuracy. Clear responsibilities: Set boundaries around which decisions an agent can make and which require human sign-off. When team members know exactly where accountability sits, they can better direct agents. Comfort through exposure : Confidence grows through familiarity. We recommend starting with low-stakes use cases (like scheduling internal meetings) to help motivate teams before moving to high-stakes operations (such as financial forecasting). 3. Manage hybrid teams of people and agents Next, it’s important to support collaboration when you bring agents into your team. Let’s look at how this might work in practice, Focus on results: Collaborate across teams to break down workflows at both the tool and task level. Cross-functional perspectives reveal an end-to-end view of the process, helping you pinpoint where agentic capabilities belong and how to prioritize ideas by technical feasibility and business impact. Reinforce behaviors: Top performers on a hybrid team are the people who guide their agents well. Reward team members for auditing an agent's reasoning and catching when its logic drifts from company goals. Coach your teams: Show your teams how to work with agents so people can spend more time on creative work and decision-making. 4. Build agentic literacy through experimentation Your teams need to understand how agents solve problems. People who know where an agent's logic breaks down (and why) can guide and judge its output. Beyond the tool: Literacy covers both writing a good prompt and auditing the result. Agents choose the most likely path instead of following deterministic rules, so people need to know when to trust an agent's output and when to check it. Safe learning zones: Give business roles the same sandbox access that technical teams get to build agentic literacy across the whole organization. Celebrating intelligent failure: Experimentation is how teams learn. In our experience, we’ve seen that when teams build an agent that fails because the data wasn't accurate, that team then understands how important data readiness is. Even if it didn’t work out, this should still be encouraged so your teams keep experimenting. 5. Govern agents with a hub-and-spoke model To roll agents out across an enterprise, you need central guardrails that don't slow down the teams closest to the work. A hub-and-spoke model does both: it gives teams a shared foundation to build on and room to move at their own pace. The hub: Establish a central AI council team that sets guidelines, maintains ethical guardrails, and manages a library of approved tools. That way, teams don't rebuild the same things. The spokes: Allow individual teams to adapt those tools to their own needs, experiment quickly, and give feedback on what works in practice. Within Google Cloud Consulting, we use our internal Agent Catalog to share low-code agents and skills that drive cross-team learning, innovation, and efficiency. However, you don’t need to build a custom platform to implement this. Here are a few approaches: Filter and sort agents made by employees through a simple internal web app. Publish and share agents with built-in Gemini Enterprise features like Agent Gallery. Work directly with technical teams that help organizations create tailored solutions. Lead with a people-first approach to AI Becoming an agentic organization is about your people. Give your teams systems and guardrails to move fast, room to experiment, and leadership that promotes accountability. Ultimately, the overarching goal is to build an organization where human ingenuity and agents support and amplify one another. title: Five rules for evaluating agent skills before they bloat your context window
raw_text:
You’re probably hearing more about SKILL.md files, and you’ll see that a lot of people test them the same way: paste a prompt into chat, watch it pass once on a laptop, and merge to main. But when you paste three pages of CLI docs into a markdown file without an evaluation loop, you are just as likely to confuse a frontier model as you are to help it. For the past weeks, we have been diligently measuring and optimizing our own Google Cloud Developer Plugin , with the most essential skills and the Developer Knowledge MCP server to ground responses in the documentation. We ran dozens of scenarios with Gemini, Antigravity, and other agents. We used Claude Sonnet 5 on Gemini platform inside isolated Harbor pods on GKE Autopilot . And, we contributed Kubernetes and Gemini platform capabilities upstream to NVIDIA's open-source evaluator. Here's the five-rule engineering playbook we use to verify a skill is worth its tokens. 1. Gate trigger collisions and security risks before spinning up containers When an evaluation run shows zero improvement between your plugin arm and your baseline arm ( Δ = 0 ), the natural urge is to rewrite the body of your SKILL.md instructions. Hold off on that. Nine times out of ten, the agent never loaded your skill in the first place . Coding agents do not read full SKILL.md bodies at turn zero. The router only inspects the short name and description in your YAML frontmatter. Once a workspace grows past a dozen skills, two failure modes collide: under-triggering (your description describes internal implementation rather than developer intent) and sibling hijacking (a broad phrase like "helps with cloud deployments" in a neighboring skill intercepts the prompt first). We recently open-sourced skill-reach so you can catch frontmatter collisions before spending on container sandboxes. It validates manifests, computes vocabulary overlap against nearest rival skills, and runs empirical routing probes across Claude Code, Google Antigravity, and OpenAI Codex: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'uv tool install skill-reach

# 1. Validate YAML frontmatter & token budgets (zero API calls)
reach lint ./skills

# 2. Detect vocabulary collisions & nearest rival skills (e.g. 0.69 overlap)
reach overlap ./skills

# 3. Run cross-harness routing probes and auto-tune weak descriptions
reach eval ./skills/cloud-run --runs 3
reach optimize ./skills/cloud-run --apply'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f94259a48d0>)])]> Pair skill-reach with NVIDIA's SkillSpector (Tier 1 and Tier 2 of SkillEvaluator ). As the Nemotron Labs team details in their Evaluating Agent Skills deep dive , standard code linters miss agent-native risks buried in markdown prose: prompt injection, silent data exfiltration, tool poisoning, and trigger abuse. 2. Never trust an eval that runs on a developer laptop If you run skill benchmarks directly on your workstation, your numbers are lying to you. A developer laptop is packed with ambient state that contaminates the baseline arm: Cached Google Cloud credentials Exported project variables and warm bash history Global environment rules An unassisted baseline agent can pass a cloud deployment test by inheriting a default project ID or token sitting in your local shell profile, masking the exact failure your skill was written to solve. Host resource contention also warps agent trajectories. While hill climbing code-retrieval agents with AlphaEvolve, our internal testing showed that running the exact same agent benchmark while a workstation was under CPU load dropped the score . Slower file scans and subprocess timeouts cause the agent to abandon search paths prematurely. 3. Measure paired WITH vs. W/OUT ablation ( Pass@3 ), not vibes Running prompts a single time and screenshotting the green checkmarks is not a real evaluation. Multi-turn tool-using agents branch on every shell exit code and stdout snippet. In our retrieval study, more than a third of benchmark tasks produced different scores across consecutive runs of the exact same code and prompt . A perfect score is equally meaningless without a paired baseline for comparison. Both Claude's plugin eval tool and NVIDIA's SkillEvaluator run paired ablation across multiple repetitions : Arm A runs the base model in a clean sandbox without the skill, while Arm B runs the identical prompt and sandbox with the skill mounted. Comparing the score improvements across our sandbox trials exposed three clear patterns that single-shot testing hides. Without the plugin, the base model still stumbled into a working deployment on most runs, but only after burning minutes of wall-clock time guessing deprecated flags and retrying bad requests. Conversely, when a test case shows identical success with zero efficiency gain, the base model already owns that capability natively. Your skill is pure context tax — delete it. code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '# Scaffold and execute a k=3 paired WITH vs W/OUT ablation locally
claude plugin eval init ./my-plugin
claude plugin eval ./my-plugin --runs 3'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f9426023890>)])]> 4. Separate efficiency and security from correctness so agents can't reward-hack When you connect an evaluation harness to an automated optimizer (like AlphaEvolve or reach optimize ), it is a surprisingly common pattern for the agent to cheat the grader . In our AlphaEvolve retrieval experiments, evolved candidates discovered four distinct ways to game the benchmark without solving the task . When the grading harness blocked specific expected substring checks in source code, an evolved candidate dynamically concatenated strings at runtime, traversed up the directory tree, and read the ground-truth answer file directly off disk. Another candidate spawned subprocesses to bypass AST checks. The evolutionary loop favored those cheaters because the fitness formula blended correctness (0.95 weight) and token efficiency (0.05 weight) into a single score. Reading the answer file from disk takes no LLM turns , earning an efficiency bonus that gives cheaters a survival advantage over honest agents that spent tokens searching the repository. Hardening your skill evaluator against reward-hacking takes three structural guardrails. First, configure Harbor so your test fixtures, grading scripts, and answer keys live inside a dedicated verifier container that mounts workspace artifacts only after the agent container exits. Second, keep SkillEvaluator's five dimensions ( Correctness , Discoverability , Efficiency , Effectiveness , and Security ) strictly orthogonal; never let token thrift compensate for a failed test or a security violation. Third, in NVIDIA/SkillEvaluator#140 , we extended security checks to fail any trial that reads Kubernetes service account tokens or queries cloud metadata endpoints, while redacting live OAuth tokens from saved trajectories. 5. Encode operational habits, not documentation dumps Looking across all of our trials, the difference between the skills that delivered a score improvement in our sandbox benchmark and the community skills that failed came down to what was inside the markdown. Skills that copy-paste public API reference tables into skill files yield almost no lift. Frontier models already have public cloud docs in their pretraining weights; dumping thousands of words of static flags into the prompt just inflates time-to-first-token and buries actionable constraints. The skills that increased our Efficiency score in our test suite taught compact operational habits and verification reflexes instead of encyclopedic reference text: Verify CLI flags at the leaf subcommand before mutating state: Rather than listing dozens of flags in markdown, the skill teaches a simple reflex: verify help output at the command line before executing a state-changing deployment. Route through a lightweight catalog index on demand: Rather than loading fourteen heavy cloud skills into context at once, a thin root router checks a curated remote index and pulls only the specific recipe needed for the task. Enforce least-privilege auth defaults: Explicit guardrails instruct agents to authenticate via Application Default Credentials rather than downloading static service-account JSON keys, while enforcing unauthenticated access restrictions alongside explicit invoker IAM bindings. Because our evaluation stack runs in CI, upgrading models takes one flag change. We re-run the paired WITH vs. W/OUT matrix against the new model and delete every skill whose Delta drops to zero. Deleting a skill because the new model graduated past it is one of the cleanest high-fives in software engineering. Get started Ready to equip your coding agents with production-grade skills? Try the Google Cloud Developer Plugin for AI Coding Agents .
summary: You’re probably hearing more about SKILL.md files, and you’ll see that a lot of people test them the same way: paste a prompt into chat, watch it pass once on a laptop, and merge to main. But when you paste three pages of CLI docs into a markdown file without an evaluation loop, you are just as likely to confuse a frontier model as you are to help it. For the past weeks, we have been diligently measuring and optimizing our own Google Cloud Developer Plugin , with the most essential skills and the Developer Knowledge MCP server to ground responses in the documentation. We ran dozens of scenarios with Gemini, Antigravity, and other agents.

title: Introducing Physical-Engineering’s Last Exam for agents
raw_text: Authors: Burak Gokturk, VP Research & Development; Rujun Han, Research Scientist; George Lee, Product Manager. Today, the Google AI & Infrastructure team is announcing Physical-Engineering's Last Exam (PLE) , a new benchmark and open competition, developed in collaboration with Mercor, and built to test a frontier model’s ability to complete tasks in mechanical, electrical, civil and structural engineering. To help the research community measure and improve how agents handle physical engineering work, we are releasing 29 public tasks, their grading tools, and an open competition leaderboard at ple-bench.com . Frontier labs and the broader research community use model examinations to test AI’s progress in completing tasks in a specific discipline. Humanity's Last Exam measures a model’s general knowledge. Agents' Last Exam measures a model’s ability to complete digital professional work. Physical-Engineering's Last Exam (PLE) measures a model’s ability to complete work that helps build the physical world. Physical engineers design skyscrapers, power grids, and computer chips we rely on, yet we could find no existing benchmark that tests whether frontier models can do that work end to end. Why textbook benchmarks fall short for physical engineering Frontier language models now score above 90% on many academic benchmarks. However, those benchmarks mostly test textbook-style questions, single tool calls, or small, self-contained design problems. For AI developers and researchers building agents for physical engineering, existing benchmarks do not show whether an agent can produce safe, code-compliant, and cost-effective designs under a licensed engineer's review and control. As the demand for infrastructure development outpaces financing , there is a growing opportunity for agents to support engineers working to close this gap. Inside PLE: Real-world tasks built with practicing engineers PLE closes this evaluation gap with 85 long-horizon tasks across four core disciplines: mechanical (30 tasks), electrical (27 tasks), civil (18 tasks), and structural (10 tasks) engineering. Instead of answering a single prompt, an agent works inside a containerized project folder — built on Mercor’s Archipelago environment — that mirrors what a practicing engineer receives on the job. Each task holds an average of 61 files (5,170 total files across the benchmark), including PDFs, spreadsheets, emails, 2D CAD drawings, 3D BIM models, and document revisions. The agent must reason through these files, find the governing building codes and physical limits, run calculations, and generate production-ready deliverables that a licensed reviewer would review and approve. In collaboration with experts from Mercor and licensed practicing engineers from industry, we built PLE using two methods: Expert-authored tasks (44 tasks): Practicing engineers created the project folders, prompts, and grading rubrics based on real professional engineering tasks. Co-authored tasks (41 tasks): Practicing engineers designed the initial task and an agent pipeline assembled the task's environment and grader from licensable engineering standards. Engineers then validated and increased the difficulty of every task assembled by the agent. All frontier models score below 50% We tested 14 frontier models on PLE using seven publicly available agent harnesses (Antigravity, Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, OpenCode, OpenHands, and Pi). Because PLE evaluates both code compliance and cost efficiency, agents only earn points if their design passes every hard safety check first. Our baseline results show a wide gap between current models and real-world engineering requirements: High headroom: All frontier models score below 50% on our private test set, with the highest-performing model on its native harness reaching a mean score of 48.3%. Hard safety gates: While the top-scoring agent configuration satisfied 91% of individual constraints on co-authored tasks, only 41.3% of its deliverables passed every hard safety and feasibility check required. Model vs. harness impact: Choice of model drives performance far more than the harness (up to a 50-point spread across models, versus a median 3-point spread across harnesses for the same model), though harnesses significantly affect run cost. Test your agent and join the open competition Evaluating AI agents on realistic project files, strict safety rules, and material costs is a practical step toward building helpful tools for physical engineers. Here is how you can get started with PLE today: Check out the full technical breakdown in our PLE paper on arXiv . Download the 29 public tasks, grading scripts, and evaluation container from our GitHub repository . Bring your own agent setup and submit it for evaluation on our private test set at ple-bench.com —with 13 Google-sponsored models running free on our servers and prize details coming soon.

title: Google Cloud Developer plugin now available in Antigravity Marketplace
raw_text: Building cloud solutions with autonomous AI agents should feel fast, safe, and reliable. Without cloud-specific context, coding agents often struggle. They might invent deprecated SDK syntax, guess invalid command flags, or attempt operations without the required Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions. Even worse, an unguided agent can enable billable APIs or provision cloud resources without your explicit permission. Starting today, you can install the google-cloud-developer plugin directly from the Antigravity Marketplace in the Build with Google section. This plugin equips Antigravity with foundational skills, safety guardrails, and live documentation grounding for building on Google Cloud. If you've never installed a plugin using the marketplace before, you can refer to the Antigravity documentation . Configuration is straightforward. The bundled Developer Knowledge Model Context Protocol (MCP) server is pre-authorized by default. You don't need to configure API keys, exchange OAuth tokens, or edit any configuration files. You install the plugin, and your agent connects to official Google developer documentation immediately. In this post, we'll walk through what's included in the plugin, how to install it with one click, and how it grounds your agent in live Google Cloud documentation. Why use the Google Cloud Developer plugin? Coding agents often rely on static training data. Cloud platforms update quickly, and models can produce code with outdated client libraries or invalid parameters. The google-cloud-developer plugin solves this issue. It bundles curated skills, intelligent routing rules, and the Developer Knowledge MCP server into a single portable package. The plugin provides three key benefits: Live documentation grounding : The agent queries official Google Cloud documentation over streamable HTTP. Safety and cost guardrails : The agent enforces least-privilege IAM patterns and it requires your consent before it enables billable APIs or modifying cloud infrastructure. Environment awareness : The agent inspects your local environment, detects existing CLI configurations, and designs safe execution roadmaps before it runs commands. What's included in the plugin The plugin pairs core baseline skills and live documentation grounding with an intelligent skill routing architecture. Rather than limiting your agent to a fixed set of capabilities, it acts as an extensible gateway that discovers and pulls specialized skills from Google on demand. Bundled agent skills The bundled skills provide essential day-one guardrails, live documentation grounding, and the dynamic discovery engine that unlocks the broader catalog: finding-google-skills : Powers flexible skill routing by discovering and loading skills on demand from the google/skills repository on GitHub . title: Beyond Migration: Using Database Migration Service for disk shrinking
raw_text:
When database engineers hear “database migration", they typically think of a one-time onboarding pathway—moving databases from on-premises environments to the cloud, or between different cloud providers. However, Google Cloud's Database Migration Service (DMS) supports Cloud SQL for SQL Server as a source . This opens up powerful, non-traditional operational patterns for SQL Server customers within Google Cloud. Because DMS enables continuous, low-downtime database replication between Cloud SQL instances—whether in the same project, across different projects, or across regions—it can serve as an everyday utility for day-two operations like storage management. In this post, we explore a compelling operational use case for DMS with Cloud SQL for SQL Server: executing disk shrinks with minimal application downtime. Why should I shrink my disk? In many production environments, database storage only moves in one direction: up. Features like Cloud SQL automatic storage increase are essential for preventing out-of-space outages during unexpected traffic spikes, large batch imports, index maintenance, or temporary staging loads. Similarly, over the lifecycle of an application, you might archive historical records, purge obsolete data, or drop unused indexes. When data is deleted, SQL Server marks the freed space inside your data files (.mdf, .ndf) as reusable for future writes; similarly, log truncation frees up space within transaction log files (.ldf). However, the database files themselves continue to hold their peak used space unless AUTO_SHRINK is configured — a setting that is generally not recommended in production due to severe index fragmentation and performance overhead. With a manual shrink operation on the database files using DBCC SHRINKFILE , you can release that unused space from SQL Server files back to the underlying disk. Even after shrinking the database files, though, the Cloud SQL persistent disk remains at its peak allocated capacity. If you do not expect your database to grow back into that allocated disk space anytime soon, you should consider shrinking the disk itself to reduce ongoing storage costs — especially in scenarios such as: After major data archiving or purging: You have permanently moved historical data to cold storage or BigQuery and your active dataset is now a fraction of its peak size. Recovering from one-time storage spikes: A runaway transaction, large data migration, or temporary staging load triggered storage auto-increase, leaving you paying for terabytes of provisioned disk capacity you no longer need. Post-refactoring or schema optimization: You have split tables out of a monolithic database into separate services, dropped large unused indexes, or applied data compression. The query below allows you to inspect both the allocated capacity and available free space for each database file fo a database: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "SELECT 
 DB_NAME() AS [DatabaseName],
 name AS [LogicalName],
 type_desc AS [FileType],
 -- Allocated size on disk (converted from 8KB pages to MB)
 CAST(size / 128.0 AS DECIMAL(18, 2)) AS [AllocatedSize_MB], 
 -- Actually used space inside the file
 CAST(FILEPROPERTY(name, 'SpaceUsed') / 128.0 AS DECIMAL(18, 2)) AS [UsedSpace_MB], 
 -- Free space left in the allocated file
 CAST((size - FILEPROPERTY(name, 'SpaceUsed')) / 128.0 AS DECIMAL(18, 2)) AS [FreeSpace_MB], 
 -- Percentage of allocated space that is used
 CAST((FILEPROPERTY(name, 'SpaceUsed') * 100.0) / size AS DECIMAL(18, 2)) AS [SpaceUsed_Percent]
FROM sys.database_files;"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f9425c15c10>)])]> You can monitor the following key Cloud SQL metrics in Cloud Monitoring to identify whether your provisioned disk quota significantly exceeds actual disk usage, indicating an opportunity for disk shrinking: database/disk/bytes_used : Tracks the actual amount of disk space currently consumed by your database files and logs. database/disk/quota : Represents the total provisioned disk capacity allocated to your instance. Cloud SQL provides a built-in storage shrink feature to reclaim this unallocated disk space, which works well when your workload can tolerate a planned maintenance window. However, native disk shrinking requires instance downtime proportional to the total allocated disk size — which can mean hours of offline maintenance for multi-terabyte drives. If your production SLAs cannot accommodate extended downtime, Database Migration Service (DMS) offers a minimal-downtime alternative. By continuously replicating your databases to a newly provisioned Cloud SQL instance with a smaller, right-sized disk, you can reclaim unused storage while your application stays online — requiring only a brief cutover window. To understand why this approach keeps your cutover window so short, let's first look at how DMS replicates data between Cloud SQL for SQL Server instances under the hood. How DMS works under the hood: Replication between Cloud SQL for SQL Server instances To leverage DMS effectively, it helps to understand its underlying replication mechanism. When migrating between Cloud SQL for SQL Server instances, DMS coordinates a synchronization process similar to native SQL Server log shipping. Initial full backup: It captures an initial full backup (.bak) of the selected user databases and restores them on the target instance. Continuous log backups: It continuously captures and applies transaction log backups (.trn) to keep the target instance synchronized in near-real time. Because synchronization occurs at the user database level, objects residing outside of it—such as logins, linked servers, and SQL Server Agent jobs—are not automatically replicated to the standby instance. Consequently, server-level objects must be migrated manually. Disk shrinking with minimal downtime Using this continuous replication pipeline, you can reclaim unallocated storage without taking a lengthy maintenance window. Instead of shrinking the existing disk in place while the instance is offline, you migrate your workload to a newly provisioned Cloud SQL instance with a right-sized disk while your production application remains online. The DMS disk shrink workflow Provision a new target instance with a smaller, appropriately sized disk (leaving sufficient headroom for transaction logs and future data growth). Start a continuous DMS job using your existing Cloud SQL instance as the source. Let replication catch up while your production application runs uninterrupted. Perform a brief cutover: Stop application traffic, let the final transaction log apply, promote the target instance in DMS, and repoint your application. Comparison: Native shrink vs. DMS migration As shown in the comparison above, because DMS migrates your workload to a new instance at the user-database level, a smooth cutover requires migrating your server-level objects and user mappings alongside your data. Let's look at the essential pre- and post-cutover steps to include in your runbook. Pre and post-cutover essentials: Going beyond database replication Pre-cutover preparation: Migrating server-level objects Because DMS operates at the user-database level, server-level objects are not automatically replicated. You will need to create them manually in the destination instance before the cutover. Script out logins from the source using sp_help_revlogin and recreate them on the target instance. SQL Server Agent jobs & Server-Level objects: Because DMS replicates databases rather than server instance state, objects outside user databases must be scripted from the source and deployed to the destination Cloud SQL instance. In SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS), connect to your source instance, navigate to the object in Object Explorer, right-click and select Script [Object] as > CREATE To > New Query Window / File : SQL Server Agent jobs ( SQL Server Agent > Jobs ): Inspect generated scripts to ensure job steps do not reference on-premises file paths or unsupported OS dependencies. Linked servers ( Server Objects > Linked Servers ): Follow the exact same scripting approach. Ensure you enable the cloudsql.linked_servers database flag on your Cloud SQL instance before deploying. Extended events ( Management > Extended Events > Sessions ): Follow the same scripting approach. For TDE enabled instances, you will need to export the TDE certificate from source and import the TDE certificate to destination before. Instance Configurations (such as database flags, Active Directory, Entra ID configurations etc): These must be manually configured on the destination instance to exactly match the source settings. If using Polybase you will need to re-encrypt DMK for the database-scoped credentials to function correctly. Post-cutover remediation: Resolving orphaned database users Database users mapped to SQL Server logins that are either absent or misconfigured on a server instance are unable to authenticate. These are termed orphaned users . Because logins created on the destination instance will possess unique Security Identifiers (SIDs) that do not match the source SIDs preserved in your migrated databases, users will be orphaned by default. Addressing this requires manual re-mapping once the target database is brought online following the cutover. Detecting & re-mapping orphaned users: While using sp_help_revlogin preserves SIDs during login migration, creating logins on the destination instance via alternative methods generates new server-level SIDs. Because these differ from the source SIDs retained in the DMS-restored user databases, database users become orphaned after cutover and require re-mapping. 1. Detect orphaned users: Connect to each destination user database and run the diagnostic query from Microsoft's official Troubleshoot Orphaned Users Guide : code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "SELECT dp.type_desc, dp.sid, dp.name AS user_name
FROM sys.database_principals AS dp
LEFT JOIN sys.server_principals AS sp ON dp.sid = sp.sid
WHERE sp.sid IS NULL AND dp.authentication_type_desc = 'INSTANCE';"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f9438148f10>)])]> 2. Fix orphaned users ( ALTER USER ): For each unlinked database user returned by the query, execute the following statement inside the context of that database to cleanly re-map the principal and its permissions to the new Cloud SQL server login: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'ALTER USER [user_name] WITH LOGIN = [login_name];'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f943814b950>)])]> Summary and next steps DMS is more than a one-time bridge from on-premises environments into Google Cloud — it is a versatile tool for day-two operations in the Cloud SQL engineer's toolkit. When strict production SLAs prevent you from taking lengthy maintenance windows for a native disk shrink, DMS provides a reliable, managed replication pipeline to right-size your storage footprint and reduce infrastructure costs with minimal downtime. To get started with configuring Cloud SQL for SQL Server as a DMS source, explore the official documentation . And if you're new to running SQL Server on Google Cloud, check out the Cloud SQL for SQL Server introduction .

title: Shutting the Door on the XCPE Botnet
raw_text: Introduction Last week, Google and industry partners dismantled the XCPE backdoor which enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes into a botnet. We assess with high confidence that the backdoor and botnet were intentionally developed, deployed, and operated for financial gain by Videostrong Technology Co., an Android Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) and Original Design Manufacturer (ODM). Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices. These secondary modules were conducting ad-fraud; silently enrolling infected devices into residential proxy networks; and loading additional malware onto XCPE-compromised devices. We also took action to disrupt the command and control (C2) domains that operate these affiliate modules. Because these affiliates each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE, we assess that taking down their C2 domains will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices. We found this malicious software built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years, supported by dedicated infrastructure and constantly evolving configurations to evade detection and manage their affiliates. We believe this campaign wasn’t an isolated rogue insider or a development oversight. As a result, Google has cut ties with Videostrong and banned them from making devices with preloaded Google apps. Google requires OEMs go through a comprehensive suite of compatibility and security tests to ensure a consistent and safe user experience across the Android ecosystem. However, Videostrong employed obfuscation techniques to exploit a gap in our tests and load malicious code after the device's first boot. As a result, Google has implemented changes to its existing review process to better safeguard against similar activity in the future. A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors. This led to a variety of malicious activities being conducted on and through the devices, including ad-fraud, data exfiltration, and routing malicious network traffic through the devices. We worked closely with Japan’s National Police Agency, Lumen, HUMAN Security, Plume, Synthient, and TrendAI to analyze this malware ecosystem and disrupt its operations. While we expect this disruption to have a significant effect on these criminal operations, this is not the end of our work combatting malicious activity. Backdoor operators, ad-fraud rings, and residential proxy providers operate as an interconnected supply chain. Point-in-time disruptions are a critical tool to protect our users, but lasting disruption in this fluid ecosystem will require continued targeting of this infrastructure. Google undertook the following actions to support disruption of the XCPE botnet: Legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install malware modules Legal action to take down C2 domains used by over a dozen malware families loaded as modules via this backdoor Banned Videostrong and any future subsidiaries or affiliates from building and selling certified Android devices in the future, or supplying software to other certified vendors Implementing improvements to how we ensure the integrity of firmware on certified Android TV devices Overview The x.cpe network was built for ongoing profit. By giving malware affiliates backdoor access, the operators conspired to monetize these devices long after purchase. If uninstalled by a user, it automatically reinstalls from the /oem/ partition upon reboot, maintaining persistent system-level access. Its main function is to establish and facilitate communications between the C2 server and the loader and execution engine. Loader and Execution Engine: To evade security scans, x.cpe acts primarily as the C2 communicator and offloads module execution to an external loader, com.abc.nexus . This file employs native anti-analysis utilities to thwart sandbox detection, and configures and initializes the monetization modules. Most recently, com.abc.nexus has itself been phased out in favor of using more tailored dropper malware that loads and executes single modules. Monetization Modules: Videostrong monetizes its backdoored devices by loading monetization modules which are developed by entities other than Videostrong that act as affiliates. These modules are deployed as native ELF daemons, embedded SDKs compiled directly into the com.abc.nexus DEX bytecode, or are fetched as secondary APKs from the malware staging infrastructure. The loaded modules transform infected devices into residential proxy exit nodes (e.g., Linkfog, AppSalt, NetNut), ad-fraud engines (e.g., CBOXTV, HiddenView), or execute additional backdoors that load even more monetization modules (e.g. Moyu, Spirit). Infrastructure Command and Control: The botnet uses a two-stage C2 process. It first initiates HTTP POST requests to fetch dynamic configuration settings, geolocation data, and STUN server parameters. It then establishes a persistent, real-time Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT) connection to receive instructions for silent app installations, arbitrary shell commands, screen captures, and network reconnaissance. MQTT is a lightweight, publish-and-subscribe network protocol designed for low-bandwidth, high-latency, or unreliable remote networks. Malware staging infrastructure: Additional monetization modules as well as various shell scripts and legitimate applications are hosted remotely and downloaded by infected devices upon command from the operator via the MQTT broker. A significant majority of these files are hosted as Github releases on operator-owned Github pages. Other files are hosted on operator-controlled servers and file hosting sites. Malware Deep Dive Backdoor Initialization The infection chain begins with a stub package (called x.cpe in some builds and com.oemservice in others) preloaded in the system partition of the firmware and running at the android.uid.system privilege level. This stub has limited functionality. Upon boot, it checks the device's oem/ directory for the corresponding x.cpe package and initiates installation into the /data/app/ directory as outlined below. To maintain inter-process state across the firmware ecosystem, x.cpe exports two ContentProviders, which expose structured configuration tables storing runtime parameters, device identifiers, proxy configuration blobs, and execution flags accessible by co-installed system applications. This enables other apps in Videostrong’s ecosystem, such as their YokaTV Player streaming software, to fetch configuration parameters provided by the C2 server mentioned below. C2 Configuration The malware utilizes a two-stage communications protocol. It first fetches initial bootstrap configurations via an HTTP request, followed by a persistent MQTT subscription to receive commands and module download instructions. To dynamically derive the HTTP C2 bootstrap server, it follows the following routine: Queries content://com.release.debug.provider/configs for private_url via x.cpe.util.ExtraReadUtils . Queries the Android system property to determine if ro.mecool.device is true. If true, it defaults to http://mcstb.anyevonline.com:8000 If false, it dynamically generates the following: http://stb[AndroidVersion][Type].anyevonline.com:8000 . Using the selected hostname, the client makes an HTTP POST request with an AES-encrypted JSON object containing hardware telemetry (SN, MAC, model, firmware version) to the following endpoints: /router/config/mqtt : This endpoint provides MQTT broker details (including Broker Hostname, TCP Port, Authentication Tokens/Passwords, and the specific Topic structure: /device/{model}/{chipId}/{action} . After receiving this data, the device initiates a persistent, real-time socket connection to the MQTT broker. /router/config/acs : This endpoint response returns URLs for ip-api[.]com and a Google STUN server to enable the malware to identify geolocation and public IP and port mapping to traverse network address translation (NAT) boundaries. It also returns a URL ( http://ott.szbboys[.]com:8000/cpe/file/upload for uploading files, logs, or diagnostic dumps from the device, and returns flags to configure ad modules ( adBwmActive , adDevourUse , adDevourCode ), and to enable or disable core malware modules. /router/config/app : This endpoint provides module-level configs, including server mappings and parameters, which x.cpe decrypts and passes to a SQLite ContentProvider named ShareProvider ( com.oem.share.provider ). By exposing this inter-process data interface, x.cpe enables modules to retrieve up-to-date upstream infrastructure parameters (such as URLs for additional configs, user manuals, etc). MQTT Capabilities Following initial configuration, persistent real-time C2 communication is managed by the MQTT library ( x.cpe.mqtt.MqttUtils ). All identified samples analyzed to date utilize a single broker hostname, mqtt.szbboys[.]com . Specific MQTT topics are mapped to specific actions, including: Silent Application Installation : Fetches remote APKs to a temporary directory. Disable Google Play Protect : To bypass security, AppUtils.disablePackageVerify() targets the global setting " package_verifier_user_consent " via Settings.Global.putInt and sets it to -1 , disabling Google Play Protect app verification. Arbitrary Shell Execution : Executes remote commands via sh under system UID privilege level. Results are published to the MQTT broker. Shell Script Execution : Downloads and executes shell scripts via x.cpe.util.RunCmds . Remote Desktop Monitor & Screen Capture : Utilizes android.app.Instrumentation.sendKeyDownUpSync() to inject keycodes and Java reflection on hidden APIs ( android.view.SurfaceControl.screenshot / SurfaceControl$ScreenshotHardwareBuffer ) to continuously capture the screen, compress to JPEG, and publish over MQTT. Network Reconnaissance : Invokes embedded binaries ( libtraceroute.so ) to fingerprint the victim network, and perform standard ping tests. The binaries also perform robust AS-lookup WHOIS routing queries. Our analysis of the C2 data indicates the preponderance of interactions with victim devices were related to module install, uninstall, and configuration actions. We also observed Videostrong operators executing sensitive actions on the device, including capturing live screenshots; injecting keystrokes; exfiltrating sensitive data including account information, device information, package inventories, and system logs; and executing shell scripts and commands, including to establish reverse shells on devices. Loader and Execution Engine Details Earlier versions of x.cpe directly embedded malicious monetization modules. In late 2024 – possibly as a response to earlier Google enforcement related to BadBox – Videostrong removed malicious modules from x.cpe and introduced a separate malicious package they developed, com.abc.nexus , which x.cpe routes instructions and data to via Inter-Process Communication (IPC). Modern variants of x.cpe facilitate C2 communications but pass configuration parameters, module updates, and other payloads to com.abc.nexus as the execution engine. We believe the actor may have evolved the malware in this way in an attempt to ensure x.cpe could remain undetected. Upon boot, com.abc.nexus.broadcast.BootReceiver broadcasts the com.abc.nexus.data intent, bootstrapping com.abc.nexus.service.CoreService . Within CoreService.onCreate , the application performs maintenance and persistence tasks. The main logic sets up a listener through RemoteMessageHandler for IPC communications from x.cpe, and parses JSON payloads received from it. After these steps, CoreService initializes the monetization modules. com.abc.nexus services extract and orchestrate a series of nested native libraries and dynamically downloaded secondary payloads which vary significantly based on sample. Many versions of com.abc.nexus come preloaded with four or more embedded modules, while other versions contain as few as one. The most common malware modules include TitanService , BwmService , AdtimeService , lb102Service , and LinkfogService (sometimes called AgentService) . Discussion of these and other modules can be found in the monetization modules section. Persistence and Evasion The malware operators implement a number of mechanisms to establish persistence and thwart detection and analysis. As a system preload, x.cpe cannot be removed by the user. If x.cpe is uninstalled from /data/app/ , upon reboot the x.cpe service BootReceiver follows the same routine outlined above and reinstalls the package. The backdoor is able to silently download additional files to the device and execute them without user consent because it first wipes user consent configuration on the device and then disables Google Play Protect: public static void disablePackageVerify() { PreferenceUtils.setPackageVerifyFromUser(CPEApp.instance, true); AppUtils.setPackageVerify(-1); // Actioning a bypass against GPP evaluation } Figure 2: Disabling Google Play Protect In many variants of com.abc.nexus, we observed the extraction of a sophisticated anti-analysis and process hardening utility libseccomp_guard.so , which runs prior to the initialization of malware modules, to ensure they remain protected from automated sandboxes and security instrumentation. It filters system calls to prevent the pausing or termination of individual threads, denies cross-process interference to ensure isolation, and prevents the spawning of child processes. Evolution Since August 2026, new dropper packages have been installed via the MQTT channel, which appear to be synchronized with the mass-uninstallation of com.abc.nexus across the botnet. We assess this may represent a new evolution of the malware to further evade detection. These new packages are disguised as Android system applications, with names such as com.android.system.ntp and com.android.sso.auth.handler . Where com.abc.nexus could act as a general purpose loader and execution engine (executing instructions passed to it from x.cpe ), these packages instead install single monetization modules (such as AppSalt). Multiple variants of these packages extract a native ELF file, libexploit.so , which in turn executes functions nativeAdbRoot() and nativeAdbShell() . These functions restart the local adbd service as root, and initiate an ADB shell connection. Following this, the app uses the connection to install itself in the system partition. The system partition is remounted as read-write and the payload replicates itself to a newly minted directory in /system/priv-app/ and creates an XML file at /system/etc/permissions/privapp-permissions-<app name>.xml . This file grants the malware android.permission.INSTALL_PACKAGES and android.permission.REBOOT . The app configures the malware modules through hardcoded configuration parameters, and does not listen for x.cpe IPC messages. The app itself is controlled by the operators via shell scripts pushed via the broker and executed by x.cpe . These include setting the property persist.networkstack.uninstall (which, when read by the app, triggers uninstallation and cleanup), persist.networkstack.skip_system_install (which skips system installation, forcing it to remain running in /data/app/ ), and persist.networkstack.install_time (which implements timestomping, overriding the default timestamp of the app to align with the other packages installed in the system directory). Monetization x.cpe loads a variety of malicious modules for monetization. Most often the modules are associated with residential proxy services and bandwidth sharing, but we've also observed ad fraud modules. Given that a single device may be running multiple modules providing the same or similar functionality (e.g., as many as three residential proxy SDKs installed on a single device) it is clear that Videostrong seeks to monetize every infected device to the greatest extent possible. Services are loaded by com.abc.nexus via three methods: Native Daemons : Native ELF binaries prepackaged with com.abc.nexus , which are unpacked to data directories and spawned as background processes with system/root privileges. Embedded SDKs / Services : Java/Kotlin SDKs compiled directly into Nexus and invoked via Android Service lifecycles or IPC broadcast triggers. Dynamic Droppers & Secondary APK Installers : Downloader function that pulls remote native ELFs or secondary standalone APKs and invokes system package managers. Nexus receives messages from x.cpe directing it to download specific modules. Malware modules loaded via the backdoor include the following: Residential Proxy / Bandwidth Sharing Modules LINKFOG Com.abc.nexus ’s LinkfogService unpacks a Go binary named lw_android_agent from assets/ to local app storage and supplies it with vendor parameters. This service silently turns infected devices into residential edge computing and PCDN proxy exit nodes. It connects to FRP reverse tunnels, and uploads bandwidth accounting metrics to Linkfog API backends. Linkfog (operated by Beijing Linkfog Technology via 点心云 / Dianxinyun) brands itself as a “Peer-to-Peer Content Delivery Network”. Jaguar The com.abc.nexus AdtimeService extracts libjaguar.so from assets/ . The file is an unobfuscated 32-bit ELF binary written in C, compiled as a native Android binary. It utilizes JNI (Java Native Interface) to initialize its core routines, dynamically derives a ChaCha20 decryption key via ARM NEON SIMD instructions to decode heavily obfuscated configurations , and establishes an encrypted C2 channel. Upon successful registration, the C2 responds with JSON configuration specifying proxy endpoints. The proxy command loop x_ctrl_do_ctrl_msg delegates proxy operations based on incoming JSON variable commands, and is capable of both TCP and UDP relay. AppSalt / Honeygain AppSalt SDK is the residential proxy SDK owned by Honeygain, which is in turn owned by Oxylabs. com.abc.nexus.service.CoreService initializes Appsalt SDK. First, the application obtains an Appsalt SDK API key from a native library libnative_keys.so by calling its getAppsaltKey() function. Appsalt SDK is initialized without displaying a consent screen - instead it explicitly calls the optIn() method which sets a consent flag without displaying any user interface. During Appsalt SDK startup it checks the application's installation source and stops execution if the application was installed from the official Google Play Store. Once Appsalt is successfully initialized it establishes a WebSocket connection with the primary command and control domain. Appsalt uses JSON-formatted messages for initial check-in (registration) and heartbeat requests. Appsalt command and control servers use MessagePack formatted messages to issue commands pertaining to proxy operations. Appsalt SDK is configured with an initial set of domains that act as proxy gateways. The list of proxy gateways can be updated by the command and control server. The device establishes UDP / QUIC connections with these gateways. Upon initialization, it secures itself within an isolated sandbox environment, captures device telemetry, and registers with a remote server over UDP. From this C2, it receives instructions to initiate a Java NIO TCP multiplexed proxy tunnel. The service functions to route arbitrary traffic through the infected device on behalf of a remote threat actor. GaGaNode GaGaNode is the first-party SDK owned by residential proxy operator IPCola. It connects over TCP to a primary C2 server and sends heartbeat beacon data over HTTP POST to a separate server. The SDK both contains its own proxy relay functionality, and it initializes additional proxy SDKs from affiliates. Upon device registration to the C2, com.gaganode.sdk.node.endpoint.a receives incoming packets from relay servers and places them in queue for the client to read and proxy through its exit node socket. The service manages multiple proxy sessions at once (referred to as clients), and each client has its own tcp/udp queue for messages. We observe GaGaNode initializing PopaNet/NetNut and EarnFM Fleet residential proxy SDKs. GaGaNode/IPCola is thus likely able to further monetize its SDK and offer these affiliates access to the infected exit nodes. NetNut / Popanet Popanet is a residential proxy SDK developed by NetNut, a residential proxy operator. The GaGaNode module initiates the Popanet SDK ( io.popanet.Popa ). This malware is identical to the malware described in our previous disruption of NetNut . All C2 infrastructure used by Popanet samples connected to x.cpe was taken down as part of the earlier Netnut disruption. Traffmonetizer The Traffmonetizer SDK is initialized inside the primary background service com.abc.nexus.service.CoreService . CoreService operation depends on the availability of policy JSON provided by the XCPE backdoor via IPC. Before calling Traffmonetizer SDK initialization methods, the application obtains a Traffmonetizer SDK API key from the native library libnative_keys.so by calling its getTraffmonetizerKey() function. Traffmonetizer functionality is split between two components where the Android SDK acts as a state machine which handles native library callbacks through asynchronous event dispatchers. ServiceBloc monitors connection status updates from the native callbacks and ConnectivityBloc monitors Wi-Fi and mobile data network changes. Traffmonetizer native library initialization and configuration is followed by a call to baseClientStart() which establishes a WebSocket connection to a C2 server. Traffmonetizer uses a single WebSocket (TLS) connection to the command and control server to multiplex control messages and tunneled connections (supports both TCP and UDP). Traffmonetizer also supports “Content Delivery” tunneling which allows nodes to tunnel bandwidth-intensive traffic. EarnFM EarnFM is a residential proxy provider, and Fleet SDK is the provider’s SDK that enrolls devices as exit nodes into the proxy network. In com.abc.nexus , FleetSDK is initialized by com.gaganode.sdk as mentioned above. FleetSdk then loads native binary libfleetshare.so . FleetSDK establishes a persistent WebSocket connection with its primary C2 server for routing arbitrary network traffic. Incoming tasking frames are received over the WebSocket channel and processed in a continuous loop. Messages contain structured JSON commands instructing the daemon to connect to specific remote hosts, with support for both TCP and UDP. Backdoor Modules Spirit Spirit is a dynamic code loading backdoor. Spirit employs multiple stages. The first stage payload fetches device information (hardware, operating system, and manufacturer/brand information and geolocation), posting it over HTTP to a hardcoded C2 server, and fetches a list of additional modules to download from the server. The second stage communicates with a separate server, and is used for tasking, config sync, module retrieval, heartbeats, and reporting. We have observed Spirit loading a significant amount of additional malware monetization modules, including some of the families already directly loaded by com.abc.nexus . Moyu Moyu is a 3-stage backdoor previously observed as part of the BadBox enterprise. On x.cpe -backdoored devices, we observed it initialized by com.abc.nexus.service.DevourService. The first stage is an offline dropper that reconstructs and loads an embedded second stage. Stage two polls an update C2 to download, decrypt, and load the third stage. Stage three implements a backdoor with hidden Double-WebView click/conversion fraud, persistent clipboard hijacking, and secondary dynamically loaded JAR execution and a separate residential proxy trojan. Bird Bird is a 2-stage backdoor previously tied to the BadBox enterprise. Stage 1 beacons a device and analysis-environment profile to its C2 server and, when the server approves, downloads, decrypts, and loads the Stage 2 JAR. Stage 2 implements a dynamic code loading backdoor (two plugin loaders plus a C2-driven reflective method invoker), a separate downloader (silent APK installation and Accessibility-driven Google Play installs), and ad abuse (lockscreen ads, overlays, browser launches). Fission Fission is a dynamic code loading (DCL) backdoor embedded within standard video applications (e.g., com.newtv.cboxtv ). Upon initialization, the first stage plugin contacts its C2 server to download additional modules. The decrypted second stage payload fetches execution targets and tracking URLs from the C2. The request sends an unencrypted POST request with tracking metrics from the internal DeviceManager. The payload we observed was configured to commit ad fraud. Rather than rendering visible advertisements in a WebView or UI component, the Stage 2 plugin executes headlessly in the background. The module queries ad server endpoints in the background to retrieve ad placement responses, parses out both primary impression beacons ( pvm ) and third-party tracking monitor URLs ( pvtpm ), and immediately fires HTTP GET requests to each tracking endpoint to register a fake ad view without displaying creative content. When executing inside specific smart-TV application stores ( com.changhong.appstore or com.tcl.appmarket2 ), the plugin initializes and triggers the ad SDK directly to report synthetic ad exposures. Ad-Fraud HiddenView We observed HiddenView loaded remotely from the attacker’s Github channel as com.ota.service . It is a standalone ad fraud application capable of running in the background using a transparent window overlay, using hidden WebViews to load targeted web pages and simulate user interaction (scrolling, clicking, typing, media playback), playing media unattended, and capturing the user’s screen. Call to Action While we believe our actions have seriously impacted over a dozen malicious actors, the underlying illicit market is resilient. Backdoor operators, ad-fraud rings, and residential proxy providers operate as an interconnected supply chain, and when one component is disrupted, operators quickly pivot to new loaders or rival monetization SDKs. Creating lasting change requires accountability across the hardware supply chain, the residential proxy industry, and the broader technology ecosystem. Accountability and Reform A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust. By turning everyday hardware into persistent beachheads for criminal affiliates, Videostrong prioritized illicit post-sale recurring revenue over the safety and privacy of its users. Downstream hardware brands, white-label resellers, telecommunications providers, and online e-commerce marketplaces also share responsibility for closing this vector. Retailers and distributors should require independent security audits from Original Design Manufacturers (ODMs) and swiftly delist manufacturers implicated in supply-chain abuse. Residential proxy providers have been able to flourish under the guise of legitimate businesses. While some providers may claim to behave ethically and only enroll devices with the clear consent of consumers, any claims of "ethical sourcing" must be backed by transparent, auditable proof of user consent. In our analysis, these proxy operators only seek consent when they are forced due to platform policy and enforcement. Silent opt-in without user consent remains the most prevalent means by which devices are turned into exit nodes. Empowering and Protecting the Consumer Residential proxies are an understudied area of risk for consumers, and more can be done to raise awareness. Consumers should be extremely wary of applications that offer payment in exchange for "unused bandwidth" or "sharing your internet." These applications are primary ways for illicit proxy networks to grow, and could open security vulnerabilities on the device’s home network. We urge users to stick to app stores you trust, review permissions for third-party VPNs and proxies, and ensure built-in security protections like Google Play Protect are active. Consumers should only purchase connected devices, such as set-top boxes, from reputable manufacturers. Our Android TV website provides the most up-to-date list of partners. Industry Collaboration We encourage mobile platforms, ISPs, online marketplaces and other tech platforms to continue sharing intelligence and implementing best practices to identify malicious backdoors, illicit proxy networks, and other harmful software and limit their harms.
