summary: Introduction Last week, Google and industry partners dismantled the XCPE backdoor which enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes into a botnet. We assess with high confidence that the backdoor and botnet were intentionally developed, deployed, and operated for financial gain by Videostrong Technology Co., an Android Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) and Original Design Manufacturer (ODM). Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices. These secondary modules were conducting ad-fraud; silently enrolling infected devices into residential proxy networks; and loading additional malware onto XCPE-compromised devices.

title: The Rise of LLMJacking: How Threat Actors Monetize Compromised Cloud and Model Resources
raw_text: Written by: Christopher Romano, Codi Starks, Garrett Mahoney, John Wolfram, Josh Murchie, K Singh, Mathew Potaczek, Mike Lombardi, Rik Dolfing Introduction Mandiant responded to multiple incidents in 2026 in which threat actors hijacked enterprise access to Large Language Models (LLMs), a tactic known as "LLMJacking." Spanning a variety of cloud and LLM providers, these intrusions impacted organizations in North America, South America, and Asia Pacific across the financial services, retail, technology, and transportation sectors. Unlike the gradual resource consumption associated with cryptojacking, LLMJacking can generate large spikes in fraudulent cloud charges in a matter of hours. Across individual incidents, we observed fraudulent charges associated with resource consumption exceeding $100,000 USD in a single day, with cumulative charges at some organizations reaching $1 million USD before access was revoked. Figure 1: Usage chart showing LLMJacking generating a spike in API requests Analyzing the criminal ecosystem behind these frontline compromises, and building upon previous reporting on the growing underground market for LLM credentials, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) has identified a diverse set of financially motivated threat clusters operating out of multiple regions globally. As the LLMJacking ecosystem matures, we are also tracking a division of labor between threat actors establishing initial access to compromised environments and operators managing downstream monetization infrastructure, known as “LLM Mixers”. LLM Mixers function as illicit routing gateways that proxy, aggregate, and resell unauthorized LLM access to underground subscribers. In one investigation, GTIG observed two distinct operational clusters coordinating to compromise and monetize enterprise LLM infrastructure, demonstrating the sophisticated specialization emerging in this space. In this blog post, we describe the attack lifecycle observed across recent LLMJacking investigations and provide actionable detection, hardening, and remediation guidance to help organizations secure their infrastructure. Initial Access While low-level resource theft has involved the manipulation of customer support chatbots to conduct unauthorized tasks like code generation, threat actors conducting LLMJacking bypass these front-end interfaces to target backend model resources directly. Specifically, they focus on either identifying publicly exposed LLM endpoints or obtaining valid LLM application programming interface (API) keys. An example of the latter can be seen in Figure 1, where a threat actor uses an automated script to verify exposure by calling the /api/create endpoint to independently run their own models on endpoints that unsuspecting users have left publicly accessible. Leaving these services unprotected not only expands an organization's traditional attack surface, but could also introduce a significant increase in hosting costs. Figure 2: Threat Actor tests publicly exposed Ollama endpoints and attempts to register their own models Across multiple LLMJacking investigations, however, the dominant initial access vector has been exposed or stolen cloud identity tokens—including IAM credentials, Service Account keys, GitHub Personal Access Tokens (PATs), and active session tokens—which threat actors leverage to establish an initial foothold into target organizations' infrastructure. For instance, in mid-2026 UNC6993 compromised a cloud instance through a misconfigured Service Account key and used this access to grant further access to an LLM API. UNC6993 also hosted a session hijacking page masquerading as an application portal to join a group of LLM users. This page tricks users into navigating to the legitimate LLM service website, and pasting their raw JSON payload containing an active access token, which was then posted to the backend API to bypass password and multifactor authentication (MFA) controls. In another instance, one threat actor gained initial entry by combining a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) to access private code repositories with the exploitation of a suspected web application vulnerability in a package running within a containerized cloud environment. Similarly, a different threat actor leveraged compromised IAM credentials of corporate users, using cloud federation tokens to programmatically generate fresh access keys to circumvent MFA requirements. In a separate incident, a threat actor was first observed accessing the environment with a compromised cloud Service Account key with broad project permissions. Beyond general cloud identity credentials, threat actors also target LLM API keys. For example, a threat actor opportunistically harvested exposed corporate LLM API keys from public GitHub repositories. Demonstrating advanced evasion tradecraft, the group conducted automated credential validation sweeps using minimal single-token requests ( max_tokens=1 ). This allowed the threat actor to stealthily confirm the viability of the stolen keys while remaining undetected by the victim’s endpoint detection and response (EDR) and SIEM volume anomaly alerts. Lateral Movement and Persistence After gaining an initial foothold, threat actors systematically work to escalate privileges, solidify access, and conduct internal reconnaissance to identify targets and further cloud credentials. To expand their access, threat actors enumerated cloud services, code repositories, and data stores for sensitive credentials. In one intrusion, a threat actor conducted internal reconnaissance across multiple cloud regions to map available services and identity policies. In a separate intrusion, a threat actor compromised a containerized cloud environment. Once inside, they performed extensive repository reconnaissance, cloning sensitive codebases to search for hardcoded secrets, configuration variables, and developer credentials. They also scanned access logs to identify credentials for secondary cloud environments. Threat actors also executed targeted database queries to harvest additional credentials; in one case, the threat actor queried cloud data warehouse metadata tables to search for database credentials, administrator passwords, and sensitive columns, alongside performing cloud object storage operations associated with targeted data theft. Across intrusions, we observed threat actors abusing cloud identity permissions and virtual machine configurations to escalate privileges and maintain persistent access. Utilizing service accounts associated with compromised workloads, one threat actor exploited token-creation privileges to generate temporary credentials for high-privilege service accounts, resulting in the exfiltration of infrastructure credentials, internal database passwords, and third-party API keys from cloud secret managers. Other threat actors established persistence by creating unauthorized IAM and service accounts and injecting SSH keys into compute instances. Specifically, one actor escalated privileges by attaching administrative policies to service roles, created unauthorized IAM accounts with full administrative rights, and established interactive management sessions into running virtual machines to inject unauthorized SSH public keys into host configuration files. Similarly, another threat actor created deceptive backdoor service accounts disguised as internal billing optimization utilities and injected environment-wide SSH keys into compute instance metadata. Beyond exploiting traditional cloud infrastructure permissions, we have observed instances of threat actors targeting vulnerabilities specifically within LLM routing software to escalate privileges. In one case, after acquiring pre-validated Virtual Keys from the threat actor that established initial access, a follow-on cluster executed targeted application logic exploitation against the victim's LiteLLM gateway. The actor exploited a user ID rebind vulnerability in the /key/regenerate endpoint (CVE-2026-40217) to elevate standard Virtual Keys into full PROXY_ADMIN master administrative credentials, establishing deep, persistent control over the compromised environment. LLM Abuse The ultimate objective of LLMJacking is the monetization and resource-hijacking of foundation models, which actors achieve through token proxying, automated model streaming, and GPU hardware provisioning. Threat actors frequently enabled a variety of managed generative platforms, and created additional API keys to scale their operations. Upon acquiring LLM API access keys, UNC6993 attempted to generate additional API keys and enable associated services within victim cloud projects, quickly accumulating over $100,000 USD in billing charges. Another threat actor subscribed victim accounts to Pay-As-You-Go agreements, selecting premium foundation models and launching high-volume inference streams. To bypass rate limits, the threat actor deployed a "burn and rotate" strategy, continuously creating and deleting short-lived service accounts while auditing the cloud provider’s billing interface to monitor financial impact. Threat actors also leveraged their access to host their own proxy endpoints and agentic workloads. For example, one threat actor enabled agents, deployed publicly accessible reverse proxies, and used custom Node.js proxy bundles to expose endpoints compatible with multiple frontier LLMs rebranded under a persona known as D1337-KAIROS . The actor deployed a containerized backdoor using the Manus agent framework to the compromised cloud environment, which queried an upstream LLM to reason through instructions and execute resulting commands locally, supported by SearXNG metasearch and agent-infra/sandbox execution environments. To scale compute, the threat actor provisioned compute instances with powerful GPUs, attempted to spin up high-end hardware across multiple regions, and requested quota increases via the cloud provider’s API. The actor also hosted LiteLLM gateways on external servers to manage and route API traffic. Rather than consuming hijacked compute solely for their own operations, GTIG observed evidence of threat actors monetizing compromised API quotas by selling access to these resources through LLM Mixers. The threat actors used open-source API gateways and custom relay infrastructure to pool stolen credentials, meter usage, and obscure the origin of the requests. For example, UNC6993 used open-source tools such as new-api (a centralized model hub and gateway) and gcli2api (an API proxy tool converting command line interface (CLI) tools into standard frontier model endpoints), likely to aggregate stolen keys and balance request loads across accounts. We believe the threat actor sells access to these tools via underground storefronts. Another threat actor that executed more than 500,000 LLM API calls in less than eight hours leveraged stolen third-party API keys to power the token routing service jet-night.com . Jet Night passed nearly one million dollars in token costs to the victim organization. Given Jet Night’s per-token costs to users are so far below typical market rates GTIG believes the service relies on stolen keys to operate profitably. For example, Jet Night offers an unlimited token plan for approximately $60 USD per month with alleged access to frontier models, a consumer service level that would typically run between $100 and $250 per month. Moreover, the service has advertised multiple outages on its public Telegram channel which is likely due to stolen keys being revoked as victims discover their respective compromises. Figure 3: Screenshot of Jet Night Plans and Pricing Structure A threat actor deployed custom proxy relay infrastructure ( ai-relay ) hosted on deceptive lookalike domains. For example, they registered a domain to masquerade as the victim's legitimate internal host. This custom relay infrastructure was used to seamlessly siphon high-value commercial LLM access into the illicit newapi[.]pro resale ecosystem, directly draining the victim's corporate account quotas to serve their underground customers. Outlook GTIG expects that threat actors will increasingly prioritize LLMJacking over traditional resource theft like cryptojacking, driven by the immediate, high-margin monetization enabled by emerging underground LLM Mixers. As enterprises integrate higher-tier models and agentic workflows into production environments, cybercriminals will likely refine automated reconnaissance to target exposed API tokens and exploit vulnerabilities in model routing middleware. This operational specialization will sustain a growing illicit resale marketplace, allowing threat actors to rapidly siphon enterprise quotas while passing the billing costs to victims before compromises are detected. Detection and Hunting In the event that security measures have failed, it is critical that defenders have early visibility into abuse of cloud LLM platforms. Defenders should prioritize detection of modifications to LLM accounts and services and treat any unauthorized enablement as a critical security event. In multiple incidents that Mandiant investigated, LLM services were not enabled at the time of compromise. Abuse of access keys allowed the threat actor to modify and enable LLM API services (e.g. Bedrock, Gemini API, etc.). Once enabled, the threat actor can use the APIs to generate massive bills to the organization in just minutes or hours. Google Security Operations Google Security Operations customers have access to these broad category rules and more under the Cloud Threats, Mandiant Frontline Threats, Mandiant Hunting Rules rule packs. The activity discussed in the blog post is detected in Google SecOps under the rule names: AWS Account Key Creation AWS Create New Access Key AWS Create User Account AWS Delete User Account Base64 Encoded Shell Command Execution Create and Delete Firewall in Default Network GCE Project SSH Keys GCP Service Account Key Creation GCP Create New Service Account GCP Firewall Rule Created Linux Archive Exfiltration via Curl or Wget Persistence: Compute Set Instance or Project Metadata Startup Scripts or URLs Mitigation and Remediation To prevent attackers from abusing Cloud LLM services, defenders should prioritize Identity and Access Management (IAM) and supply chain security, two of the most common pathways for gaining access to and abusing Cloud services. Credential Hygiene : Utilize a centralized secrets management platform to control the management and rotation of sensitive keys and secrets. Automation of secrets and keys can limit the lifespan of leaked credentials. Least Privilege : Ensure users and service accounts only possess the permissions necessary for their specific role and required tasks. Deny all permissions that are not explicitly required, including access to Cloud LLM services. Code Monitoring : Automate secret scanning within codebases (GitHub, Gitlab, etc.) to ensure API keys and secrets added to source code are identified and removed promptly. Routine Configuration Audits : Perform periodic comprehensive configuration audits of Cloud services to identify potential attack paths and unintended exposure of endpoints. Rate Limiting : Implement a WAF like Google’s Cloud Armor to enforce rate limiting for individual client connections. Network Allow Listing : Restrict outbound connections from Cloud services via VPC firewall rules to known IP addresses where feasible. Budget Alerts : Implement granular API quotas on LLM services to limit request volume per model. Utilize spending caps to set budgets and avoid over-spending. Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA): Enforce phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication across all cloud identity providers, management consoles, and developer platforms to ensure that stolen credentials or session tokens cannot be easily exploited. Shadow LLM Discovery: Utilize Security Posture Management tools to automatically scan your hybrid cloud environments and identify unauthorized or unmonitored tools, models, and infrastructure, ensuring complete visibility of your model footprint. Granular API Key Scopes: Restrict and segment API keys by specific model endpoints, environments (dev/prod), and usage limits to ensure a compromised token for a basic utility model cannot be used to invoke expensive, high-tier frontier models. Validation Sweep Monitoring: Monitor model gateway and API access logs for anomalous, low-volume requests (such as max_tokens=1 or zero-temperature pings). Attackers frequently use these micro-transactions for stealthy credential validation sweeps prior to launching large-scale infrastructure abuse. Vulnerability & ML Supply Chain Patching: Integrate automated vulnerability scanning (SAST/DAST/SCA) across your custom application code, containerized workloads, and machine learning dependencies (like PyTorch and Hugging Face libraries) to prevent initial access via unpatched server vulnerabilities. Gateway Patch Management: Extend vulnerability management programs to include centralized model proxy and routing gateways (e.g., LiteLLM), ensuring rapid patching against privilege escalation and authentication bypass flaws (such as CVE-2026-40217). Sandboxed Execution for Dynamic Workloads: Isolate the runtime environment in highly virtualized, process-isolated, serverless sandboxes if your LLM application is required to execute generated code or database queries dynamically. Vetted Model Repositories: Restrict and enforce model pulls and pipeline dependencies solely from trusted internal registries or approved enterprise catalogs to prevent developers from pulling compromised models containing pre-configured backdoors. Graph-Based Exposure Modeling: Implement continuous, graph-based risk prioritization that maps cloud assets, application code, and data flows to automatically identify and remediate complex, multi-hop attack paths. Adversarial Exposure Validation: Deploy automated offensive agents to continuously test external attack surfaces, uncover exposed endpoints, and simulate credential validation sweeps. Monitoring Native Cloud Audit Logs AWS : Monitor CloudTrail logs for API events from bedrock.amazonaws.com . Based on historical LLM Jacking incidents, monitor for the following API operations across the attack lifecycle: Resource Exploitation : Monitor for direct execution of the LLM via the Converse , InvokeModel, and InvokeModelWithResponseStream API operations. API Throttling & Error Spikes: Monitor for high-volume spikes in ThrottlingException , ValidationException , or ResourceNotFoundException errors, which could indicate an automated “spraying” methodology targeting cloud infrastructure. Target Scoping : Monitor potential reconnaissance activity used to discover available models via the ListFoundationModels,ListInferenceProfiles , and GetFoundationModelAvailability operations. Additionally, monitor for attempts to unlock new models in the environment via the PutUseCaseForModelAccess and CreateFoundationModelAgreement API operations. Security/Evasion : Review attempts to view, alter, or disable logging configurations to conceal prompt contents and avoid detection. Monitor the GetModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration operation, as well as PutModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration and DeleteModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration . Any calls to disable logging by non-IaC (Infrastructure as Code) principals should be treated as high severity. Automated Tooling: Analyze User-Agent strings to identify automated tools and SDKs (e.g., claude-cli, aws-sdk-rust, and aws-sdk-go-v2) interacting directly with the target cloud infrastructure. Azure : Monitor Azure Activity Logs (Control Plane) and Diagnostic Logs (Data Plane) for events associated with the Microsoft.CognitiveServices namespace. To hunt for or detect LLM Jacking incidents, monitor the following operations: Resource Exploitation : Monitor for direct execution of the LLM. In Azure, model invocations occur on the data plane and require Diagnostic Logs to be enabled. Look for high volumes of POST requests to inference endpoints such as Completions or Chat Completions APIs. On the management plane (Activity Logs), monitor for unauthorized creation of new instances via the Microsoft.CognitiveServices/accounts/deployments/write operation. Target Scoping : Monitor potential reconnaissance activity to discover available Azure LLM resources, models, and deployments via the Microsoft.CognitiveServices/accounts/read and Microsoft.CognitiveServices/accounts/deployments/read operations. Security/Evasion : Review attempts to view or modify logging configurations (to see if data plane model invocations are being recorded) via the Microsoft.Insights/diagnosticSettings/read , Microsoft.Insights/diagnosticSettings/write , or Microsoft.Insights/diagnosticSettings/delete operations. GCP : Monitor Cloud Audit Logging for calls to Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform endpoints (aiplatform.googleapis.com). Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform inference operations are contained within Data Access logs, which are disabled by default due to volume and ingestion costs. You must manually configure your IAM audit policies to track these. Enablement of Agent Platform Services : Alert on enablement of Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform services via the google.api.serviceusage.v1.ServiceUsage.EnableService method. Resource Exploitation : Monitor for direct execution of the LLM via Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, which requires Data Access audit logging to be enabled. Look for google.cloud.aiplatform.v1.PredictionService.Predict , google.cloud.aiplatform.v1.PredictionService.GenerateContent , and google.cloud.aiplatform.v1.PredictionService.StreamGenerateContent operations. Target Scoping : Monitor potential reconnaissance activity to discover available models and endpoints via the google.cloud.aiplatform.v1.ModelService.ListModels , google.cloud.aiplatform.v1.EndpointService.ListEndpoints , and google.cloud.aiplatform.v1.PublisherModelService.ListPublisherModels API operations. Security/Evasion : Review attempts to view or alter logging and audit configurations. Monitor for operations like google.iam.v1.IAMPolicy.GetIamPolicy (to check if Data Access logs are enabled on the project/resource) or attempts to review log exports via google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.ListSinks and google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.GetSink . title: CrowdStrike’s AI SOC vision evolves as agentic uncertainty adds new twist
raw_text: “The software we use has become an actor,” declared CrowdStrike President Michael Sentonas in his address on the dangers and opportunity of agentic AI at the company’s Fal.Con conference in September. It’s an idea that until recently would have been dismissed as absurd, yet across cybersecurity it’s now taken as a given. For decades, the adversary has been nuisance hackers, professional cybercriminals, or well-resourced teams working for nation states. The arrival of rogue agents — underlined by real-world incidents such as OpenAI’s infamous assault on Hugging Face — has demolished this. Agents still work on behalf of humans, but they don’t always reason or act like them. They are entities with capabilities and an unpredictability unlike any threat businesses have ever faced. “I believe we just crossed a line. Agents have escaped evaluation environments and compromised infrastructure they were never supposed to touch,” Sentonas told the crowd in Las Vegas in early September. “For decades, software did what we programmed it to. It has moved from execution to agency.” Sentonas’ point wasn’t simply that malicious agents are a threat. The arrival of agentic AI also raises larger questions for security operations centers (SOCs), which will deploy agents on a scale that matches or even exceeds attackers. That makes agents a threat from both the outside and inside the enterprise perimeter. “What happens when millions of AI agents act at machine speed on both sides?” Behind the confident marketing pitches from CrowdStrike and a growing cast of rivals, the honest answer right now is that nobody can be sure. Coming from a cyber vendor, Sentonas’ reference to “millions” of agents might sound like a number meant to hype the threat. But it is likely no exaggeration, with Gartner forecasting that the number of agents used inside a single Fortune 500 company will expand from 15 in 2025 to 150,000 by 2028. “As CIOs and IT leaders see an explosion of AI agents across their organizations, many are contending with an ungoverned sprawl of agents that expose their organizations to a range of risks, including misinformation, oversharing, and data loss,” says Matt Goss, a senior director analyst at Gartner. Taking up the agent challenge For years, Fal.Con was about persuading enterprise SOCs to consolidate capabilities under CrowdStrike’s do-it-all Falcon platform, comprising nearly three dozen modules. In 2023, with its “Raptor” release, Falcon and the company’s flagship event took a hard turn toward AI . In this changed world, AI wasn’t simply a Falcon capability; increasingly it was Falcon, influencing everything it did. The AI theme dominated Falcon’s 2026 Fall release , bringing the company’s growing portfolio of AI SOC capabilities under the Falcon umbrella with the launch of the Agentic Security Platform. Most individual components — Charlotte AI AgentWorks, Model Context Protocol (MCP) Integration, the AI-enabled Enterprise Graph — were announced in 2025 as part of the company’s Agentic Security Workforce plan but a closer look reveals important new features. Currently, agents investigate alerts using pre-built Falcon agents or custom agents built using the no-code AgentWorks solution. Charlotte AI now gives these agents a shared memory layer in Enterprise Graph that enables them to coordinate with one another across multiple endpoints, identities, and cloud services simultaneously (aided by the company’s 2025 acquisition of Onum , which accelerated the speed with which agents can ingest data). On paper, the effect is to dramatically speed up alert triage while expanding the scope and capacity of worker agents in a way that relieves human SOC teams of a lot of basic grunt work, including some Level 2 investigation and Level 3 remediation and hunting workflows. Also new is SafeMind , a frontier red-teaming system based on Nvidia’s Nemotron open-weight LLM, comprising offense (Red Tempest) and defense (Blue Solano). This agentic framework continuously tests an isolated mirror of the live environment for weaknesses, feeding the results back into detection at the agent level. CrowdStrike didn’t invent the concept, but it does appear to be the first to integrate an autonomous testing model into a SOC platform. Speed is not enough This might look brand new, but the early incarnations of the agent-powered SOC are as much evolution as revolution. Everything inside a traditional CrowdStrike-powered SOC — from its Falcon EDR sensor, Enterprise Graph data, and cloud-native management — remains in place. Humans are still essential to decision-making, albeit at a higher level than before. What agents add to this SOC paradigm is a new abstraction layer separating SOC teams from the mass of telemetry they have increasingly struggled with. This should be good news for defenders because it means they have some hope of matching the speed and scale of agentic attacks. But speed is only the beginning, points out James Patrick, CTO for the FIOR Group, which develops an AI policy and security gateway. “Attackers and defenders can both operate at machine speed, so simply making SOCs faster isn’t enough. We need to move beyond reactive detection towards continuous testing of our defenses.” SOCs must work out how much they delegate to agents and what constraints are set around this. “Enterprises already struggle with fragmented telemetry, overlapping security products and inconsistent policies. Adding autonomous systems introduces another problem: establishing who or what has authority to act, and how to verify that authority,” says Patrick. According to Chris Cochran, field CISO and VP of AI security for the SANS Institute, that’s why “for most organizations, agentic AI will be augmentative rather than a replacement for analysts, at least for the next few years.” Agent platforms, including CrowdStrike’s, still have work to do proving themselves in terms of oversight and governance. “The core problem is that we’re applying a probabilistic technology to a discipline that usually requires determinism,” Cochran adds. “A SOC needs to know that the same input will produce the same action, and that the action can be explained to an auditor or an incident review board.” For that reason, Cochran believes that while agentic-powered SOCs will remove a huge amount of alert handling and correlation effort, the workload will shift to processes such as verification. “Teams should continuously evaluate agents against known-good and known-bad cases, the same way you’d regression test detection content,” he says. “None of this is exotic, but it takes engineering time that many SOCs haven’t budgeted for.” Enemy within One deeply unfamiliar problem is that agents themselves are an emerging attack surface within the enterprise and must be constantly assessed. Traditionally, security tools defend the environment, and the idea that an agent system doing the same job could itself become a direct threat is new. But what makes agentic AI unsettlingly is its non-deterministic nature, which means that, unlike a traditional security tool, it has the potential to do things you didn’t tell it to and haven’t planned for. “Organizations are deploying autonomous systems that access sensitive data, use privileged identities, interact with applications, and execute actions. Those agents can be compromised, manipulated, or behave unexpectedly,” says Tom Findling, CEO and cofounder at AI SOC startup Conifers.ai. “Security operations will need visibility into agent identities, permissions, actions, and decision-making processes, and the ability to detect and contain dangerous behavior.” CrowdStrike’s answer, relaunched at this year’s Fal.Con, is Falcon Guardian, an AI detection and response (AIDR) solution featuring runtime enforcement, agent discovery, execution graph mapping prompts, and quarantining for misbehaving agents. Similar capabilities will be needed for any agent platform but the mere fact that security systems now need their own security systems underscores what CrowdStrike’s Sentonas was referring to with his software-as-actor remark at Fal.Con. Human SOCs need to protect their enterprises from their AI SOC helpers. To that end, CrowdStrike yesterday announced the roughly $400 million acquisition of Fiddler AI , an AI agent monitoring and governance vendor from the emerging, burgeoning, and somewhat confusing agentic AI tools ecosystem . Fiddler’s platform tracks AI models’ behavior, attempting to provide explanations for their actions as a means for establishing a control plane for governing and securing them. Its 100-plus metrics track hallucinations, toxicity, personally identifiable information (PII) leakage, and drift, enforcing policies to protect against jailbreaks, prompt injections, and bias. Enterprises deploy tools like Fiddler to make model drift visible and actionable before it becomes systemic risk . CrowdStrike intends to bundle Fiddler into its flagship platform as Falcon Observe in Q4 FY2027, approximately six months from now, as a means for “proving businesses can safely use AI agents every day,” according to Sentonas’ post announcing the acquisition . CrowdStrike has invested heavily in agentic AI, building an impressive stack of capabilities that extend the Enterprise Graph that made it a dominant player capable of surviving the occasional embarrassing global hiccup . It has even embraced a degree of openness, allowing data ingestion, API connectors, and partnership gateways to enrich the data going into its Falcon AIDR. However, there’s no getting away from Falcon as the single control plane. “CrowdStrike starts with endpoint security and an established enterprise security platform. Other vendors approach the problem through identity, networks, cloud, or security analytics. They all have an incentive to bring customers further into their own platforms,” observes FIOR Group’s Patrick. “The challenge for CrowdStrike, and for every vendor, is that a platform can’t independently verify itself,” he adds. “What’s needed is control that is genuinely independent of any single platform and works across those boundaries.” According to Patrick, a critical feature will be the ability not simply to deploy a security layer but to continuously assess its security and performance. As the traditional detection and remediation stack of cybersecurity is pushed out of shape, the growth in new layers and processes could make this task almost as demanding as the main job of cyber defense that agents were supposed to simplify.

title: Barracuda’s security appliances have a security problem of their own
raw_text: Barracuda, which offers a wide variety of cybersecurity devices, has been bitten by a bug itself. The company has disclosed two critical and high-severity vulnerabilities that, if chained together, could allow threat actors to bypass authorization controls and gain root access to devices. They consist of a pre-authentication authorization bypass vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-116606 (rated a critical 9.3 severity on the common vulnerability scoring system), and a command injection vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-111560 (rated an 8.6 high-severity on CVSS). Attackers need to have access to the admin interface of a susceptible device to successfully exploit these vulnerabilities. Barracuda has released security patches, which it advises customers to apply immediately. The vulnerabilities impact numerous popular Barracuda products Root access on an email gateway puts the attacker in the place that every inbound and outbound message passes, said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research. It may also expose the credentials and connections the gateway uses to reach the mail server and directory. “Those are the keys to the kingdom, if you will,” he said. CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560 both impact Barracuda’s Email Security Gateway (ESG), but CVE-2026-111560 also impacts its Web Security Gateway (WSG), Web Application Firewall (WAF), WAF Control Center (WCC), Load Balancer Application Delivery Controller (ADC), and Message Archiver (BMA), the company said. Customers using these products should verify that their systems are running the latest firmware versions and have received all security patches, it advised. The device will show the latest firmware version available; if a device’s firmware is multiple versions out of date, users may need to perform several updates. Enterprises whose appliances’ admin interfaces are not publicly accessible from the web are less exposed, Barracuda said; the company advised restricting access to these interfaces to trusted internal networks and applying appropriate network access controls to limit exposure. “The biggest concern is how these two vulnerabilities could chain together,” said Jon Nelson , principal advisory director at Infotech, noting that an attacker who can bypass authentication and then exploit command injection could move from accessing an exposed appliance to executing commands on it. “Assessing each vulnerability in isolation can understate the risk,” he said. Dickson added that security leaders should read the advisory closely, as it calls one flaw “pre-authentication,” then lists “Authentication Required: Yes, administrative access.” “Both cannot be true in the usual sense,” he pointed out. Likely access here means being able to reach the admin interface over the network, without a password. “If your admin interface faces the internet, that condition is already met,” Dickson said. The advisory also labels a 9.3 severity rating as “high,” when 9.0 and above is actually “critical” on the standard scale, he pointed out. “These are small things, but labels drive patching queues,” he noted. Also, the advisory does not say whether these flaws are currently being exploited, but it does not say they are not, either. How enterprises should respond “Get the admin interface off the internet,” Dickson emphasized, noting that, as a cybersecurity consultant, he gives that advice at least a handful of times a week. “Management interfaces on edge devices are continually a source of vulnerability .” Once teams limit admin access to a trusted internal network or a dedicated management network, Dickson advised, they should then “verify the patch rather than assume it was properly installed.” From there, he said, analyze for unauthorized visitors by reviewing admin logs, check for unfamiliar accounts, and look for unexpected outbound connections from the device. History matters here, he added. In 2023, after a zero-day on this same email security gateway (ESG), Barracuda told customers with compromised appliances to replace them outright rather than rely on the patch. As he put it: “A patch fixes the lock. It does not tell you who already has a key.” Nelson agreed that enterprises should look closely at who can reach their administrative interfaces. They should, in addition, put access behind additional controls such as a properly configured zero trust access layer. “Exposing those interfaces directly to the internet was always a bad idea,” he said. “As AI makes it easier to find weaknesses and chain attacks together, that exposure becomes increasingly difficult to justify.” AI is also expanding the search for software flaws to include issues such as business logic weaknesses where an application can be made to bypass its intended controls. Authentication and authorization bypasses deserve particular attention in that context, Nelson said. As more vendors use advanced AI to examine their code, CISOs should prepare for more flaw disclosures and potentially shorter windows to respond to them, he noted. “That means identifying exposed appliances, restricting access, and having a response plan ready before the next zero day arrives,” he said. Understanding what each appliance exposes Security appliances are increasingly creating vulnerabilities in corporate networks, which is changing the cybersecurity discussion. Enterprises rely on them to protect the network, yet ultimately they are software systems with vulnerabilities of their own. “They sit exactly where attackers want to be,” Dickson noted. Firewalls, VPNs, and email gateways face the internet by design; that is their job, he said. They see sensitive traffic and hold credentials. Most cannot run the endpoint detection tools that protect laptops and servers, so a compromise can remain undetected for a long time, and every customer runs the same firmware, so one working exploit can scale to thousands of organizations. “The discussion is shifting from which box to buy to what the box itself exposes,” Dickson said. “Every appliance purchase is a decision to trust a vendor’s code at the most exposed point in the network.” It deserves the same scrutiny as any other in an enterprise, he noted. Buyers should ask their vendors four questions, he advised: Is the admin interface exposed to the internet by default; how quickly do patches ship; are they applied automatically; and what logging can users see? “The security appliance does not just protect the perimeter,” Dickson pointed out. “It is the perimeter, and it should be treated as the most attacked system an organization owns, because it is.”

title: Node-RED authentication hole being exploited in the wild
raw_text: Months after Siemens released fixes for an authentication hole in flow-based programming tool Node-RED, it remains unpatched by many users and attackers are taking advantage of it in the wild. The problem involves open source IoT/IIoT systems, including those embedded in critical infrastructure, deployed outside the control of CISOs and CIOs. Security firm VulnCheck discovered the exploits and disclosed details in a blog post on Monday . “On October 30, 2026, one of our canaries caught an attacker exploiting CVE-2026-58115 , an unauthenticated Node-RED admin API flaw, to deploy a flow that downloads and runs a Linux bot. The request came from an IP in Microsoft’s ASN (AS8075),” the post said. “We have since seen 16 events from the same IP against this CVE, covering several different payloads.” The core problem is that Node-RED ships with the authentication option disabled; users are supposed to change the setting before it goes live. Patrick Garrity , the VulnCheck security researcher who wrote the post, said the fact that Node-RED deployments are popular among those outside IT makes them susceptible to unsophisticated errors like this. “They are put in place by relatively nontechnical people,” Garrity said in an interview. Aman Mahapatra , chief strategy officer for New York City-based technology consulting firm Tribeca Softech, said the Node-RED hole is not new, but it is still being leveraged in the wild. “The condition being exploited is one Node-RED has carried for years as a default: unless an administrator configures authentication, anyone who can reach the editor can deploy flows, and the project’s own documentation says as much,” he said. “Node-RED is popular precisely because engineers can wire it up without involving IT, which also means it rarely appears in an asset inventory. It is the same pattern behind this week’s supermarket refrigeration attacks : equipment installed outside the security team’s view, reachable from the internet, with authentication switched off.” Mahapatra pointed out that the biggest danger is the nature of the way users tend to deploy Node-RED. “It is integration middleware. A typical deployment speaks Modbus, OPC UA, MQTT or S7 to controllers on one side and to databases, brokers and cloud services on the other, and it stores credentials for all of them,” he said. “A compromised instance is a credential vault for every system it touches and a bridge across an IT/OT boundary that the network diagram says does not exist.” Another problem is that industrial system patches tend to happen on pre-planned schedules, rather than responding to emergent issues or suggested setting changes. “Siemens published its advisory on August 11, and VulnCheck caught exploitation on October 30, three days after shipping its own detections,” Mahapatra said. “Eleven weeks is a short runway in OT, where firmware updates wait for planned maintenance windows, so a meaningful share of affected gateways will remain unpatched well into next year.” Frank Dickson , principal analyst at Dickson Research, added that the details of the exploits are a good news/bad news situation for CISOs. The good news is that the attacks did not appear to have targeted industrial systems. The bad news is the attackers found and accessed those systems anyway. Noah Kenney , principal consultant at Digital 520, agreed. “They don’t necessarily need to understand the equipment or operations connected to these gateways. They’re simply looking for systems capable of executing their commands,” he said. “That creates a concerning possibility where industrial operations could be disrupted by attackers who never intended to target critical infrastructure in the first place. Even generic malware consuming system resources or interfering with network communications could have operational consequences.” Dickson added that closing this hole may not resolve the exposure. “The report also found that some attackers skipped the bot and left web shells, hidden back doors for running commands later,” Dickson said. “Patching closes the door. It does not evict anyone already inside.”
summary: Months after Siemens released fixes for an authentication hole in flow-based programming tool Node-RED, it remains unpatched by many users and attackers are taking advantage of it in the wild. The problem involves open source IoT/IIoT systems, including those embedded in critical infrastructure, deployed outside the control of CISOs and CIOs. Security firm VulnCheck discovered the exploits and disclosed details in a blog post on Monday . “On October 30, 2026, one of our canaries caught an attacker exploiting CVE-2026-58115 , an unauthenticated Node-RED admin API flaw, to deploy a flow that downloads and runs a Linux bot.

title: Critical Langflow flaws enable authentication bypass and RCE
raw_text: IBM patched critical vulnerabilities in Langflow, an open-source framework for building AI agents, LLM-powered workflows, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems. The flaws could allow attackers to bypass authentication, leak API credentials, and execute arbitrary code. Langflow, now owned by IBM, is popular in enterprise environments because it offers a visual experience that doesn’t require coding knowledge to create AI workflows and agents. Vulnerabilities in the framework have been exploited in the wild to steal AI and developer credentials before, most recently in August . This latest round of security patches fix four vulnerabilities , two of which are rated critical with 9.8 CVSS score. One flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-93680, stems from an incomplete remediation of a previous auto-login security issue. Exploiting it could allow attackers to bypass security restrictions and gain access to features that would normally require authentication. Another flaw, CVE-2026-110186, allows unauthenticated remote attackers to execute arbitrary code through Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool enumeration. A third vulnerability, CVE-2026-110193, which is rated as high severity, also allows for code and command execution on the server due to an issue in a third-party library used by the Agentic Assistant. However, exploiting this flaw requires authentication with at least a low-privileged account. The fourth vulnerability, CVE-2026-110192, is an information disclosure issue due to insufficiently protected API credentials. It is rated as 6.5 on the CVSS scale. The flaws affect Langflow OSS versions 1.0.0 to 1.12.8 and were fixed in the newly released 1.13.0 version, which is available both from the PyPI repository and as a Docker image. “Before upgrading, back up the database, secret key, and uploaded files,” IBM said in its advisory. “If the deployment uses automatic login, prepare the existing account for password sign-in as described in the installation and Docker upgrade instruction.” The company also released patches for three medium-severity flaws in Hono, an API and web application development framework used inside Langflow for request routing and backend web server tasks. The company advises users to upgrade Hono to version 4.13.5.

title: UK organisations warned to brace for AI-powered ransomware attacks
raw_text: AI-powered malware is “highly likely” to be used in ransomware attacks on Britain’s critical national infrastructure within the next two years. The head of GCHQ’s National Cyber Security Centre, Dr. Richard Horne, warned that abuse of AI technologies is making it much easier for attackers to rapidly expose and exploit long-neglected security weaknesses. Dr. Horne argued that underinvestment in technology and security have left organisations carrying a technical debt that leave them wide open to attack. AI adoption by hostile actors is “highly likely” to increase the scale and efficiency of their operations, including ransomware attacks, social engineering, and vulnerability exploitation, the latest edition of the NCSC’s State of the Cyber Nation annual report warns. The issue is more that AI will allow attackers to exploit overlooked vulnerabilities rather than forge exotic new attacks. The report identifies state-linked threat groups, particularly China and Russia, as the UK’s primary cyber antagonists. For example, in July 2026 the NCSC warned that Russian groups were systematically exploiting vulnerable routers and globally targeting networks maintained by critical national infrastructure providers, including energy grids and telecommunications networks. In August 2026 the NCSC warned about increased targeting of operational technology systems across multiple sectors globally, including in the UK. “AI will continue to be integrated into threat actors’ cyber operations, increasing the speed, scale and efficiency of existing attack methodologies rather than autonomously conducting end-to-end attacks,” the NCSC report predicts. The NCSC reports that up to 88% of all attacks originate from just four vectors: phishing, exploiting public-facing applications, misuse of valid accounts, and exploiting external remote services. Variations on a theme “None of these vectors are radical or new,” said Oliver Spence, CEO of security operations tools vendor CybaVerse. “In fact, they represent the same failures cybercriminals have successfully exploited for decades.” Spence added: “Threat actors rarely depend on the most complex, technical means for launching attacks; more often than not, they search for the most easily exploitable holes in organisations’ systems, like misconfigured VPNs and vulnerabilities in third-party vendor software platforms, and on tried-and-true social engineering techniques.” AI doesn’t represent a sea-change in attackers’ strategies but rather a force multiplier. “Threat actors may be able to leverage AI to launch more sophisticated attacks, but the real danger is in the automated exploitation of existing weaknesses and organisational failures,” Spence concluded. Countermeasures AI offers a means to improve the UK’s collective cyber resilience, but it will only be effective if organisations deal with years of underinvestment and foundational weaknesses before building from a more solid foundation, according to Dr. Horne. The UK government’s Cyber Essentials scheme should become the starting point or baseline for enterprise cyber security, not the end goal, for building improved cyber resilience. Last week the UK government pledged £70 million for a new National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre, which will be task to identify vulnerabilities across critical infrastructure and the economy, and a new AI Cyber Security Centre of Excellence, run by the NCSC.

title: Network appliances go more than a year without patches as exploits speed up
raw_text: The median vulnerability on enterprise network appliances stays unpatched for more than a year, Microsoft’s own telemetry shows, even as the most damaging software flaws are being weaponized within days of disclosure. Microsoft Security Research reported the findings Monday in an analysis of roughly 383,000 CVEs disclosed from 1999 through September 2026. It shows that the median time to patch a vulnerability exceeds a year for network appliances. The period is more than a month for Windows servers, over 10 weeks for Linux servers and applications running on macOS, and about two weeks for Windows workstations. “That gap is the threat actor’s window, widest on the critical systems that stay exposed the longest,” Microsoft Security researchers Yair Tsarfaty and Or Begam wrote in a blog post detailing the findings. They were referring to the distance between how fast flaws are exploited and how slowly critical systems are patched. Patching measured in weeks and months Microsoft drew its patching figures from 2026 data in its Security Exposure Management product. The median vulnerability is fixed in about two weeks on Windows workstations but takes more than a month on Windows Server, according to the post. The delay stretches beyond 10 weeks on Linux servers and for applications running on macOS, and past a year on network appliances . Vibhum Dubey, a cybersecurity researcher and red teamer, said the findings reflect what he sees across enterprise environments. In those environments, change approvals, application dependencies, maintenance windows, and legacy infrastructure routinely hold up fixes. “Network appliances are particularly difficult because firmware upgrades can affect critical business operations,” Dubey said. “In many cases, the challenge is not identifying vulnerabilities, but getting the right teams to remediate them without disrupting business services.” Exploitation measured in days Exploitation runs on a far shorter clock, Microsoft wrote in the post. Citing CISA figures, the researchers said the mean time from CVE publication to listing in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog fell from 89 days in 2024 to 57 days in 2025. For 2026 through September, the mean has dropped to 20 days and the median to three. “Exploitation runs on the opposite clock: the most impactful vulnerabilities are weaponized in days, increasingly on or before disclosure,” the post said. The researchers also cited VulnCheck’s State of Exploitation 2026 report, which found that 29% of exploits in 2025 were launched within a day of CVE publication. Industry research points to advances in AI as a significant factor in cutting the time needed to develop exploits , Microsoft wrote in the blog post. In some cases, defenders have hours rather than weeks, Dubey said. Vulnerabilities can be exploited before public disclosure or before organizations have completed their initial assessment. He said enterprises need to move away from relying entirely on monthly scans and scheduled patch cycles. In their place, he said, they need continuous monitoring, emergency patching procedures, virtual patching through WAF and IPS controls, and clear remediation ownership. “The priority should be to reduce the window of exposure, because by the time a vulnerability reaches the regular patching queue, attackers may already be exploiting it,” Dubey said. Where the exploits land The vulnerabilities attackers actually use look very different from the CVE population as a whole, the analysis found. Server-side remote code execution (RCE) flaws make up 20% of all published CVEs but 37% of those exploited in the wild. Local privilege escalation climbs from 11% to 18%, and client-side RCE from 4% to 13%. Cross-site scripting drops from 15% of published CVEs to 4% of exploited ones, and denial-of-service flaws drop from 16% to 7%, according to the researchers. Operating system vulnerabilities make up 23% of the overall population but account for 41% of exploited CVEs. “These patterns are consistent with threat actors favoring vulnerabilities that can provide meaningful access and control,” the researchers wrote. Together, RCE, authentication bypass, and local privilege escalation account for 78% of real-world exploited vulnerabilities, the post said. Windows ranks as the most affected platform among exploited CVEs in Microsoft’s data. Prioritizing by exposure A vulnerability’s value to an attacker depends on its impact and its exposure, according to Microsoft. Impact is what successful exploitation delivers. Exposure is the identities, privileges, and network connections reachable from the compromised asset. Servers frequently run service accounts, application identities, or cloud-managed identities with more permissions than they need, the post noted. Taking over one of them can open paths to sensitive data, administrative rights, and trusted networks. “CVSS scores alone are no longer sufficient,” Dubey said. Organizations should prioritize vulnerabilities based on active exploitation, internet exposure, asset criticality, and potential attack paths, he said. “A medium-severity vulnerability on an internet-facing system with a known exploit can present a greater risk than a critical vulnerability on an isolated asset,” he said.
summary: The median vulnerability on enterprise network appliances stays unpatched for more than a year, Microsoft’s own telemetry shows, even as the most damaging software flaws are being weaponized within days of disclosure. Microsoft Security Research reported the findings Monday in an analysis of roughly 383,000 CVEs disclosed from 1999 through September 2026. It shows that the median time to patch a vulnerability exceeds a year for network appliances. The period is more than a month for Windows servers, over 10 weeks for Linux servers and applications running on macOS, and about two weeks for Windows workstations.

title: Enterprises pay $100,000 a day for AI they never ordered
raw_text: Enterprises deploying large language models (LLMs) in production may be unknowingly footing the bill for someone else’s AI business. Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) is warning of financially motivated LLMjacking campaigns in which cybercriminals hijack enterprise cloud and model access before reselling it through underground subscription services. The activity can generate fake cloud charges exceeding $100,000 in a single day, GTIG said in a blog post . In some incidents, cumulative charges reached $1 million before organizations revoked the compromised access. “LLM Mixers turn stolen enterprise model access into a service for paying customers, while the victim’s systems continue accepting requests through credentials they recognize,” said Piyush Sharma , co-founder and CEO at Tuskira. “That puts a lot of weight on the authority attached to each credential. A key issued for one application shouldn’t become a reusable pass to other models and workloads.” GTIG’s analysis is based on multiple incidents in 2026, spanning a variety of cloud and LLM providers across North America, South America, and Asia Pacific. Stolen model access becomes an underground business GTIG said the monetization infrastructure centers on LLM Mixers, criminal routing gateways that aggregate compromised API credentials and resell model access to underground subscribers. These services proxy requests across stolen accounts, distribute consumption and hide the original source of access. Multiple operations were identified using open-source gateways and custom relay infrastructure to pool stolen credentials. One threat actor, UNC6993, used tools including new-api and gcli2api to aggregate stolen keys and distribute requests across accounts. Another operation used stolen third-party API keys to power Jet Night, a legitimate token-routing service that executed more than 500,000 LLM API calls in under eight hours, GTIG said. The activity passed nearly $1 million in token costs to the victim organization. Jet Night advertises unlimited access to frontier models for approximately $60 a month, substantially lower than the typical cost of comparable legitimate access. Jet Night also experienced occasional outages that GTIG suspects were caused by victims discovering compromises and revoking keys. “Selling stolen model access gives criminals a reason to keep that access working for as long as possible, which makes the quiet activity before the spending spike especially important,” said Nick Tausek , lead security automation architect at Swimlane. “By the time someone asks why the cloud bill has exploded, the attacker may already have paying customers.” The attack begins long before the bill arrives Initial access involves exposed or stolen cloud identity tokens, including IAM credentials, service account keys, GitHub personal access tokens, and active session tokens, GTIG pointed out. Attackers also harvest LLM API keys from public repositories and scan for exposed model endpoints. Attackers were seen validating stolen keys with minimal single-token requests, sometimes using max-tokens=1. Such micro-transactions can confirm whether credentials work while remaining below conventional consumption-based detection thresholds. “Testing a stolen key with a single-token request barely registers as consumption,” Tausek said. “But pair that request with a newly created credential or an unexpected permission change, and there’s something worth investigating.” Analysts shouldn’t have to pull those connections together manually while the attacker gets a head start, he added. After establishing access, attackers enumerate cloud services, repositories, and data stores for additional credentials. They may escalate privileges, create unauthorized service accounts, inject SSH keys, or establish persistence through compromised workloads. GTIG observed a follow-on threat actor exploiting a user ID rebinding vulnerability in the LiteLLM gateway to elevate ordinary virtual keys into administrative credentials. Sharma said organizations must restrict credentials to their intended models, workloads, and endpoints. “The gateway compromise described in these incidents deserves particular attention,” he said, warning that control of the routing layer could open access beyond the original compromised credential. GTIG recommends tighter credential management, least-privilege permissions, granular API key scopes, monitoring for suspicious low-volume requests, and spending limits on model consumption. It also urges organizations to monitor unauthorized AI service enablement and gateway vulnerabilities.

title: Armed with AI, hackers target endpoint security blind spots, raising stakes for CISOs
raw_text: A China-linked hacking group’s use of AI agents to identify security weaknesses during a global espionage campaign is raising concerns about whether enterprises can detect gaps in their defenses before automated attacks exploit them. CrowdStrike reported that the group, tracked as VAPOR PANDA, used an AI-powered penetration testing framework called ARTEX to target more than 200 organizations worldwide over an 11-day period beginning October 17. The organizations included government agencies and businesses across at least 14 countries, with researchers confirming post-exploitation activity at nine. At a global pharmaceutical company, the attackers instructed AI agents to examine running processes and folder listings on Windows machines to determine whether CrowdStrike’s Falcon sensor was installed, according to transcripts recovered by the cybersecurity firm. ARTEX uses multiple AI agents to carry out intrusion tasks under human direction. CrowdStrike found that VAPOR PANDA used the framework to pursue attacks against several organizations simultaneously, with operators intervening at key decision points. The findings follow an October 21 report from Microsoft detailing a separate campaign involving ARTEX. Microsoft said another China-linked group, Storm-0940 , used the framework to automate attacks targeting hundreds of organizations, gaining privileged cloud access in less than three hours in some cases. The campaign included the abuse of compromised ConnectWise application credentials to access customer environments. Changing economics of cyberattacks The use of AI in cyberattacks is changing the economics of state-sponsored espionage by allowing smaller teams to pursue targets without a corresponding increase in personnel, according to Akshat Tyagi , associate practice leader at HFS Research. “The techniques are familiar, but the ability to run them in parallel is not,” Tyagi said. Jonathan Ong , senior analyst for managed security services at Omdia, said AI can substantially reduce the time attackers spend on reconnaissance, even as more sophisticated exploitation continues to require technical expertise. The attacks documented by CrowdStrike exploited weaknesses that security teams have encountered for years. At a Greek government organization, attackers used authentication keys from a 2022 directory export that had likely not been rotated. At a US pharmaceutical company, an AI agent combined an unsigned SAML assertion with an XML external entity (XXE) vulnerability to obtain a cloud role with extensive administrative permissions. Security gaps become a bigger target Growing concerns about the security risks of AI adoption should not distract organizations from established defensive measures, Ong said. Tyagi added that CISOs should ensure that security monitoring extends across their environments rather than assuming existing deployments provide complete coverage. Amit Kumar Jena , development manager for AI at Kanerika, said organizations should continuously measure endpoint protection coverage, including on internal servers, and generate alerts when machines stop reporting to security monitoring systems. He also recommended enforcing SAML signature validation and restricting cloud access privileges. Security teams should watch for closely sequenced authentication attempts and commands that could indicate automated malicious activity, he said. Tyagi also recommended regularly rotating credentials and monitoring unusual account activity, warning that automated attacks leave defenders less time to investigate suspicious behavior. Keith Prabhu , CEO of Confidis, said gaps between security systems could give attackers opportunities to move through enterprise environments. He recommended improving asset visibility and detecting suspicious activity across systems rather than relying on individual security controls. Prospect of Cobalt Strike-style adoption The use of ARTEX by different threat groups also points to the wider availability of tools capable of automating cyberattacks. CrowdStrike said VAPOR PANDA used ARTEX with DeepSeek and a second commercial AI model. Although the framework’s developer withdrew the original open-source project in October following reports of its misuse, copies and modified versions remain available. Tyagi expects such tools to become more widely adopted by financially motivated cybercriminals over the next 12 months. There is already evidence of broader adoption. In research published in October, Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant said they had observed financially motivated attackers using ARTEX during data-theft extortion operations, alongside its use by suspected state-linked groups. “AI pentesting frameworks such as ARTEX have the potential to become the Cobalt Strike of the AI era,” said Ong. Cobalt Strike , a commercial penetration-testing tool, has been widely abused by cybercriminals and state-sponsored groups. As attackers automate more of their operations, security teams may need to rely more heavily on automated detection. Tyagi said this would allow analysts to spend less time manually reviewing alerts and concentrate on decisions requiring human judgment. Prabhu said CISOs should prioritize faster, rehearsed incident response rather than simply investing in additional AI tools or expanding security teams. Such preparations could help security teams respond to intrusions in which automated agents explore multiple attack paths before defenders have completed their initial investigation. Although ARTEX can automate much of an intrusion, the observed campaigns still involved human operators directing key decisions. “We are not at fully autonomous attacks yet,” Tyagi said. The continuing role of human operators does not diminish the speed of the attacks. For security teams, the challenge is detecting suspicious activity early enough to prevent automated intrusion attempts from developing into broader compromises.

title: 67% of security leaders say their teams struggle to meet business needs
raw_text: AI, identity-based attacks, and expanding digital operations are putting pressure on already overstretched cybersecurity teams. Security vendor Barracuda’s Cybersecurity Skills Gap report also found that security teams are struggling to keep pace with expanding responsibilities. The vast majority of the 2,000 IT and security decision-makers surveyed report cybersecurity skills gaps. In particular, the most common challenges are linked to AI-related risks (68%) and advanced identity and phishing threats (67%), including business email compromise , OAuth abuse, and multi-factor authentication bypass. Two-thirds (67%) of respondents say security teams are under pressure and struggling to scale to meet evolving business needs. Half say their security professionals are expected to support growing digital operations without additional resources. More than half (56%) report a reduction in security head count linked to AI, split evenly between entry-level and more senior roles. As AI takes on more routine analysis and response activities, human roles are shifting toward (higher value) threat investigation, incident leadership, automation governance, and business risk management. “AI is changing the cybersecurity landscape faster than many security teams can build the necessary skills, visibility, and governance,” said Siroui Mushegian, senior vice president and chief information officer at Barracuda. “Organizations need to reshape their security teams, combining the power of AI and automation with human expertise, judgment, and visibility.” Hiring challenges CSO parent company Foundry’s forthcoming Security Priorities report found that cloud security (35%), securing agentic AI technology (34%), and securing AI/machine learning-enabled technology (30%) topped the areas CSOs felt their teams needed to become more skilled and knowledgeable about in order to meet overall corporate security objectives. Underlining the difficulty of this ambition, the report found that cloud security architects, AI security specialist, and forensics analysts were the most difficult cybersecurity roles in which to find suitable applicants. Accessing the cost of the skills gap Separately, technology-focused online learning platform Pluralsight’s Tech Skills Report 2026 found that 41% of cybersecurity professionals in the UK estimate skills gaps cost them at least £380,000 each year (US$500,000). This estimated cost includes hiring and outsourcing expenses, lost revenue, abandoned projects, and poorly maintained technology. A quarter of cybersecurity professionals say their organization has experienced security incidents or vulnerabilities over the past 12 months due to skills gaps. Almost half (43%) admitted that skills gaps are a common reason for abandoning cybersecurity projects. The findings highlight the pressure on security teams as AI adoption increases demand for cybersecurity expertise, Pluralsight concludes. AI imperative exacerbating skills problem Europe is short of more than 300,000 cybersecurity professionals, and companies are now struggling to find qualified candidates or applicants, according to research by the AI Workforce Consortium . Cybersecurity job postings requiring AI skills have doubled year over year across G7 countries. Senior cybersecurity roles requiring AI skills are up 65% year-on-year, compared with 5.9% for junior roles. The research by the AI Workforce Consortium — an industry group backed by Cisco, Google, Microsoft, IBM, SAP, and others — also points to a growing need for practical experience and human skills.

title: European supermarkets that failed to act after French freezer attack are now feeling the heat
raw_text: Just a couple of weeks after a cyberattack on French supermarket refrigeration systems resulted in spoiled food, and even some fires, retailers in Belgium, Ireland, Sweden, Finland, and Estonia were hit with nearly-identical attacks on Monday. The mid-October attack prompted an advisory from the French Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-FR) recommending that organizations disconnect any refrigeration control systems with public IP addresses from the internet, and to reconnect them via a secure VPN only after verifying the configuration and, if necessary, restoring factory defaults. In an emergency, the advisory suggested, organizations could simply filter connections to allow only the IP addresses of their refrigeration suppliers or service providers to connect, but this should not be a long-term solution. The Monday attack, like the one in October, “resulted in sudden changes in the temperatures of their fridges and freezers,” according to a Bloomberg report , which confirmed incidents with impacted retailers, including Carrefour, Spar, and Ahold Delhaize. No group has as yet claimed to be behind the attacks. A spokesman for Ahold Delhaize told CSO, “On Monday, November 2, we identified an incident affecting refrigeration systems in dozens of Delhaize stores. We immediately took the necessary measures to limit the impact and keep the stores operational.” The situation has since returned to normal, although the company had to discard valuable food, he said. Delay understandable Analysts and consultants said the lack of an immediate response to the initial refrigeration attacks is understandable, given the complex nature of the systems and the multiple vendors who typically manage such systems for major retailers. Gartner Distinguished VP Analyst Katell Thielemann said that although the impacted European retailers own the hardware, they outsource the maintenance, upkeep, and the management. Thus, she said, “there is some confusion about who owns what in this black box of outsourcing.” IDC Senior Research Manager Bobby Kuzma agreed. “There’s a huge gap in visibility between the folks who monitor threat intelligence and vulnerability reports, and the people who manage the OT/industrial side of the universe,” he said. “The cybersecurity teams may not have even been aware that the devices were network connected, especially if they were riding on dedicated internet circuits for manufacturer support.” Thielemann added that the incident was made worse because of the historic lack of priority given to cybersecurity defenses in retail. “It’s proof that cybersecurity is still not top of mind,” she said. “Even when it’s so egregious, senior [retail] leaders are not asking, ‘How do we get ahead of this?’” However, Kuzma argued, this problem comes down to asset inventory visibility. “You can’t protect a system that you don’t know you have. You can’t scan for exposures on a connection that you don’t know exists,” he pointed out. “Sometimes that inventory requires somebody physically going into the telco closet at the locations and asking pointed questions about equipment that’s present. In this day and age, having devices of any type hanging off a public internet connection and accessible is asking for trouble.” IoT handled outside of IT David Neuman , an executive advisor with consulting firm Acceligence, also noted that it was never realistic to assume that issuing a cybersecurity advisory was going to meaningfully address this security hole. “An advisory doesn’t fix a system nobody in the building owns,” Neuman said. “Contractors often install and service store refrigeration controllers under arrangements that rely on a constant data feed, so they can sit outside the security team’s inventory and authority. Taking the controllers offline means finding them, then reworking how the contractor gets in, store by store.” That, he said, “explains the gap, but it doesn’t excuse it: France gave everyone a three-week warning. Abusing a legitimate function like defrost causes physical and financial damage without any malware.” Brian Levine , a partner at consulting firm Control Risks, added that another part of the problem is that IoT devices have always been handled outside of IT. “For years, organizations treated connected operational equipment as a facilities issue. These incidents end that debate,” Levine said. “Security professionals never dismissed this risk; budgets deprioritized it because nothing had failed at scale. Now it has, and boards will ask why vendor contracts, incident response plans, and tabletop exercises never accounted for a physical outcome.” And, said Noah Kenney , principal consultant at Digital 520, this issue goes beyond the fact that the attackers could gain access. He said that he is most concerned about the range of things the attackers were able to do with that access. “The attackers could reportedly manipulate refrigeration systems to operate far outside their intended parameters,” Kenney said. “Even if someone gains access to a system, there should be independent safeguards preventing commands that could damage equipment or disrupt operations. The fact that remote access can potentially translate into physical damage suggests some serious gaps in how these systems are designed and secured.” Kenney also noted that some of these devices had long passed their end-of-life, meaning that security patches and other upgrades may have been unavailable. “Organizations can end up relying on equipment that still functions perfectly well operationally, but can no longer be adequately secured,” he pointed out. “That creates difficult decisions about network isolation, compensating controls, and ultimately when equipment needs to be replaced.” Indeed, said independent technology analyst Carmi Levy , some in IT tend to ignore IoT systems, especially when they were deployed by functional units without permission from IT or cybersecurity teams. “Enterprises don’t tend to look at fridges in the same light as servers, smartphones, and other traditionally connected devices,” he noted. “If anything, most IT shops have a limited view of what constitutes a connected device in the first place. That means many organizations are running connected devices, such as appliances, floor cleaners and once-dumb but now increasingly smart machines, with dangerously outdated firmware because they never identified them as connected in the first place.” Unexpected threat to IT As well, said Frank Dickson , principal analyst at Dickson Research, there are also corporate legal issues that may undercut cybersecurity’s need for quick action. “CERT-FR’s own alert shows why that takes time. Before cutting a controller off the internet, it tells operators to check the insurance terms in their contract with the refrigeration provider. That one line says a lot,” he said, adding that many of these controllers are installed, monitored, and guaranteed by a contractor who depends on the data feed. The store may have neither the ability nor the authority to shut them down. “Three weeks of warning is a long time for an attacker and a short time for a supermarket chain. Close the door to the internet first and renegotiate the contracts second,” he said. Dickson also argued that these refrigeration attacks pose an unexpected threat to traditional IT systems as well, because servers and other equipment are temperature-sensitive. “An attacker who reaches the building management system does not need to touch a single server. The servers will shut themselves down rather than cook,” Dickson said. “You do not need to hack the data center. You only need to hack the air conditioning.”
